title: Non-stationary low-flow frequency analysis with mixed Weibull components and Copula-based dependence framework
authors: Farhana Sweeta Fitriana; Svenja Fischer; Gabriele Weigelhofer; Johannes Laimighofer; Gregor Laaha
abstract: Abstract. Extreme low flows are a pressing challenge for water management, reducing water availability and degrading water quality. Reliable design estimates are therefore essential. Traditional low-flow frequency analysis relies on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, which is increasingly violated under climate change and by varying low-flow generating processes. In a seasonal snow-influenced climate, annual low-flow extremes may occur in both summer and winter, potentially exhibiting seasonal dependence that challenges conventional modelling approaches. This study extends traditional low-flow frequency analysis to non-stationary conditions by jointly accounting for temporal trends, seasonal heterogeneity and inter-event dependence. Building on previously developed mixed distribution and mixed copula frameworks, we generalise these frameworks to non-stationary conditions using three-parameter Weibull distributions. Seasonal low-flow distributions and their joint mixture vary over time, with linear non-stationarity in the location parameter and in inter-event dependence. Results are presented for more than 700 catchments from the European Reference Observatory of Basins for INternational hydrological climate change detection (ROBIN) dataset. Model evaluation shows that neglecting non-stationarity when present can lead to biased assessments of low-flow severity, particularly for higher return periods. In contrast, non-stationary models provide a more realistic representation of evolving low-flow regimes by revealing temporal changes that remain hidden from traditional estimators. By preserving the conceptual consistency of the previous stationary framework, the proposed non-stationary framework improves the statistical characterisation of extreme low flows and provides an enhanced basis for low-flow frequency analysis by offering new insights into past and current low-flow processes under climate change.
research_question: How can low-flow frequency analysis be extended to non-stationary conditions accounting for temporal trends, seasonal heterogeneity, and inter-event dependence?
main_finding: Non-stationary models better represent evolving low-flow regimes and reduce bias in severity assessments compared to traditional stationary models.
theme: Hydropower and water resource management under climate change

title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: Extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: Daiki Goto; Hector Manuel Lopez Rios; Monika Scholz; Suriyanarayanan Vaikuntanathan
abstract: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient "ghost" remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed-point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone-without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings-can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.
research_question: How does neuromodulation-inspired gating affect associative memory network capacity and stability?
main_finding: Neuromodulator-like gating expands memory capacity, prevents catastrophic breakdown, and creates a continuum of attractor states.
theme: Neural computation and memory networks

title: Melanosome evolution shaped sensory biology and terrestrial adaptations in early aquatic vertebrates
authors: Daniel J. Cirtina; Beatriz Carazo del Hoyo; Shaun P. Collin; Maria E. McNamara
abstract: The photic environment is a key driver of fish ecology that shapes adaptations to aquatic habitats. The evolutionary history of these adaptations, however, is difficult to trace. Melanosomes, melanin-rich organelles, offer unique insights into physiology and ecology and often fossilise. Here, we present a comparative analysis of melanosomes from extant and fossil fishes to trace the evolution of ecological and physiological adaptations through deep time. Melanosomes from internal tissues of extant fishes exhibit highly conserved geometries in all major taxonomic groups examined, indicating persistent functional constraints during evolution. Larger, more abundant melanosomes in lungfish likely reflect adaptations that underpin the vertebrate water-to-land transition. In contrast, eye melanosomes exhibit lineage-specific patterns. Bony fishes possess cylindrical eye melanosomes associated with retinomotor movements, photoreceptor protection, and improved visual acuity, whereas jawless and cartilaginous fishes possess only spheroidal melanosomes, consistent with visual sensitivity and alternative light-regulation strategies including pupillary modulation. These taxonomic differences are preserved in fossils from the late Carboniferous Mazon Creek biota, indicating that links between melanosome morphology and function were established during the early evolutionary history of these lineages in the Ordovician, approximately 445 million years ago. Early innovations in melanin biology uniquely facilitated vertebrate sensory evolution and ecological diversification.
research_question: How did melanosome evolution influence sensory biology and terrestrial adaptations in early aquatic vertebrates?
main_finding: Melanosome morphology is conserved across fish taxa and linked to ecological and physiological adaptations, with distinct patterns in lungfish and eye melanosomes reflecting evolutionary transitions.
theme: Evolutionary biology and sensory adaptation in aquatic vertebrates

title: Evaluation of vaccine-induced anti-lipopolysaccharide antibodies against clinically relevant Klebsiella pneumoniae strains to inform vaccine design
authors: Robert M. Lawrence; Nathalie Karaky; Emma Bownes; Edward Hildebrand; Cristina Alaimo; Domenico Maione; Francesca Micoli; Kathryn E. Holt; Kelly L. Wyres; David Goldblatt
abstract: Abstract Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis in low- and middle-income countries and is increasingly multi-drug resistant, highlighting the need for vaccines. Putative vaccine targets include the lipopolysaccharide (O antigen) and capsular polysaccharide (K antigen), but capsule may mask O antigen and limit antibody-mediated opsonophagocytosis. We evaluated the activity of O antigen-specific antibodies induced by a tetravalent bioconjugate vaccine against 146 clinical isolates representing 17 prevalent capsule types associated with neonatal sepsis. Susceptibility to antibody-mediated killing varied by capsule type: four were consistently susceptible, six showed heterogeneous responses, and seven were resistant despite remaining susceptible to K antigen-specific antibodies. Killing of susceptible strains was predominantly mediated by anti-O1 antibodies, as demonstrated by competitive inhibition with purified polysaccharides. Collectively, these findings support an antigen-sparing vaccine design strategy, in which susceptible capsule types may be replaced by a single O type, reducing vaccine complexity while maintaining broad functional coverage.
research_question: How effective are vaccine-induced anti-lipopolysaccharide antibodies against diverse Klebsiella pneumoniae strains for vaccine design?
main_finding: Anti-O antigen antibodies show variable killing efficacy depending on capsule type, with some capsule types susceptible and others resistant.
theme: Vaccine design against bacterial pathogens

title: Distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL captured by cryoEM reveal structural principles governing fusion activation
authors: Gonzalo L. González‐Del Pino; Richard M. Walsh; Chanyoung Lee; Hunter C. Russell; Doina Atanasiu; Tina M. Cairns; Wan Ting Saw; Gary H. Cohen; Ekaterina E. Zheleznova Heldwein
abstract: Abstract Orthoherpesviridae infect most humans for life and cause myriad diseases. These viruses distribute cell-entry functions among receptor-binding proteins such as gD, the conserved membrane fusogen gB, and the gH/gL heterodimer, which couples receptor engagement to gB activation. Here, we report cryoEM structures of HSV-2 gH/gL, including complexes with four antibody fragments, in distinct conformational states. Structural analysis suggests that these structures represent pre-activation and intermediate states rather than a post-activation state. Antibody binding appears to shift the gH/gL conformational equilibrium of gH/gL, either stabilizing the pre-activation state or promoting refolding into intermediate or post-activation-like states. Two regions – the N terminus and a domain H2 switch – adopt distinct conformations and may transmit the activating signal from gD to gB. We propose that receptor-bound gD displaces the gH N terminus, initiating allosteric rearrangements that culminate in switch refolding and may help release prefusion gB from an autoinhibited gH/gL-gB complex. Switch conservation suggests that this activation mechanism may be shared across Orthoherpesviridae . These findings uncover structural principles governing gH/gL-mediated activation of membrane fusion.
research_question: What are the distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL and how do they govern fusion activation?
main_finding: CryoEM structures reveal pre-activation and intermediate states of HSV-2 gH/gL and suggest a mechanism for fusion activation involving conformational changes.
theme: Molecular virology and structural biology of viral fusion proteins

title: Propagating shocks and transitions across networked food systems: Insights from multiplayer microeconomic modeling
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: Benjamin F. Zaitchik; Sauleh Siddiqui; Belay Simane; Ying Zhang; Sriram Sankaranarayanan; Craig Bakker; Steven Witkin
abstract: Accelerating global change is affecting coupled natural ecosystems and human activities in every part of the world. The local and regional expressions of these changes are a product of interacting and networked systems such that a shock, trend or development transition in one region, ecosystem, or sector can propagate impacts to other regions, ecosystems, and sectors. Informed adaptation and development strategies require an understanding of how signals propagate through these coupled systems and regions. Here, we synthesize findings from our work in Ethiopia and Mali, where we developed and applied a modeling system designed to capture cross-sector dynamics of networked food, water, and energy systems at subnational scale. We approach the problem using a multiplayer microeconomic model that accounts for diverse objectives through chains of food production, distribution, and consumption that connect resource regions to market regions. This paper draws lessons from three case studies in Ethiopia and one in Mali that are designed to examine impacts of a subnational climate shock (drought), a centralized national policy decision (export restrictions in response to food shortage), a distributed development strategy (solar-powered groundwater irrigation), and an external intervention (food aid). In each case, we consider how an initial signal propagates through the country via markets, infrastructure, and interactions between economic actors. An understanding of this propagation can inform strategies for food security in a changing climate.
query: reservoir management; energy storage flexibility; renewable energy land use
research_question: How do shocks and transitions propagate across networked food, water, and energy systems at subnational scales?
main_finding: Modeling shows that shocks like droughts and policies propagate through markets and infrastructure, affecting interconnected regions and sectors.
theme: Energy-system planning and integration within coupled food-water-energy networks

title: Organic matter composition modulates its degradation under the combined effects of iron (oxyhydr)oxides and light
authors: Dawei Cai; Yandi Hu; Caroline L. Peacock; Suona Zhang; Xudong Yang; Wen Liu; Peng Zhang; Quan Chen; Bo Pan; Jinren Ni
abstract: The extent of organic matter (OM) degradation in sunlit surface soils and shallow marine sediments is critical to global carbon and nitrogen cycling. Association with iron (oxyhydr)oxides can reduce degradation, but the role of light in iron–OM interaction is underexplored. Here we show that OM composition determines contrasting responses to iron and light. Carboxyl- and/or hydroxyl-containing OM undergoes oxidation and decarboxylation, releasing carbon dioxide, whereas protein-like carboxyl–amine OM forms cross-linked products through condensation and polymerization, with only limited degradation. Iron and light promote oxidation–decarboxylation by enhancing electron transfer and visible-light absorption, while iron promotes protein unfolding and light may provide energy for polymerization. Under high-irradiance conditions equivalent to one-month cumulative daylight exposure, a conditional assessment of representative sunlight-exposed topsoil OM indicates potential carbon losses of ~8% for carboxyl- and/or hydroxyl-type OM versus ~1% for carboxyl–amine-type OM. Photochemically promoted amide formation may limit OM degradation and carbon loss, informing carbon management and process-based carbon cycle models. This study shows that iron minerals and sunlight drive different fates for organic matter in soils and sediments depending on its chemistry: some forms are broken down and lose carbon, while others form cross-linked products that resist degradation.
research_question: How does organic matter composition influence its degradation under combined effects of iron (oxyhydr)oxides and light?
main_finding: Organic matter composition determines contrasting degradation responses to iron and light, with some types undergoing oxidation and carbon loss, while others form resistant cross-linked products.
theme: Carbon cycling and organic matter degradation influenced by mineral-light interactions

title: Integrating surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes: A systematic review and research framework
authors: Guangxi Ding; Jia Qin; Shiqiang Zhang; Bingfeng Yang; Junhao Cui; Feiteng Wang; Jianfeng Yang
abstract: Abstract. Climate warming has accelerated permafrost degradation, leading to significant challenges in water circulation and transformation. Since the early 21st century, especially during the last ten years, permafrost hydrology has garnered substantial attention, yielding a wealth of research outcomes. However, a comprehensive and systematic understanding of the permafrost hydrology remains limited. This study synthesised the current knowledge through an extensive literature review and systematic analysis, establishing a foundational framework for permafrost hydrology. The framework integrated three critical dimensions: surface hydrological processes, hydrological functions of the active layer, and the hydrological effects of permafrost changes. Subsequently, the current state, trends, and challenges in permafrost hydrology research were summarised, and a holistic overview was provided. Regarding surface hydrological processes in permafrost regions, this study examined the impacts of freeze-thaw cycles on surface runoff from multiple perspectives, including the influence of active layer thawing, slope hydrological processes, river channel dynamics, large-scale permafrost hydrology, and the hydrological consequences of thermokarst formation. For hydrological processes within the active layer, the study identified the hydrological role of the active layer, key factors influencing its hydrological behaviour, and the interactions between suprapermafrost water and soil water. Concerning the hydrological impacts of permafrost thaw, this study investigated the transformation dynamics between surface and groundwater in permafrost regions by analysing the effects of climate change through increased baseflow, groundwater recharge, and subsurface runoff. Finally, this study outlined future research directions, emphasising three key areas: the application of novel observational methods, integrated surface-subsurface investigations, and the ecological and environmental impacts of permafrost hydrological changes.
research_question: How can surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes be systematically integrated and understood?
main_finding: A foundational framework integrating surface hydrological processes, active layer functions, and permafrost change impacts was established through systematic review.
theme: Hydrological impacts of permafrost degradation and climate change

title: Dynamically adaptive soft bioelectronics for neuro-immunomodulatory cancer therapy
authors: Wenliang Liu; Jingjie Liu; Renyuan Sun; Ming Yang; Dingke Zhang; Kun Yang; Weixian Xu; Chuan Gao; Shihao Wang; Ziyu Zhang; Qiong Wang; Wenyuan Wang; Qingya Liu; Lei Zhang; Jiexiong Feng
abstract: Abstract Many solid tumors remain refractory to immunotherapy due to profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments. Although vagus nerve stimulation offers a direct neural axis to reprogram immune function, its potential in cancer immunotherapy remains unrealized due to the absence of stable, system-level neuromodulation platforms. Herein, we develop a miniature subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulator (SVNS) for near-organ neuromodulation of pancreatic tumor immunity. To construct stable electrical coupling with subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve (SVN) along the esophagus, a dynamically adaptive neural interface comprising an injectable anti-fatigue adhesive conductive hydrogel and a deformable liquid metal electrode is explored. The SVNS is integrated with a battery-free lead-free wireless power module, which can be configured into a Swiss-roll architecture, enabling minimally invasive implantation. In an orthotopic mouse model of pancreatic tumor, chronic SVN stimulation using SVNS suppressed tumor growth and metastasis, reshaped tumor innervation, promoted a shift toward an M1-like TAM phenotype, enhanced cytotoxic immune cell infiltration, and further potentiated the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.
research_question: Can subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulation modulate pancreatic tumor immunity to enhance cancer immunotherapy?
main_finding: Chronic subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulation suppressed tumor growth and metastasis and enhanced immune response in a pancreatic tumor mouse model.
theme: Biomedical neuro-immunomodulation for cancer therapy

title: Differentiating Westerly and Asian monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean since the late Pliocene
authors: Yi Yang; Fei Yu; Jingtao Zhao; Xue Ding; Panfeng Li; Shuang Wang; Xiaoyan Ruan; Xiaoqiang Yang; Thomas J. Algeo; Bangqi Hu; Shucheng Xie
abstract: Asian dust flux is a fundamental regulator of global climate and marine biogeochemical cycles, yet it is difficult to separate the dust fractions delivered to the tropical Pacific Ocean by the Westerlies and East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM). We present a 4-million-year record of eolian evolution from the Philippine Sea to deconvolve these two distinct transport systems on the basis of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting. Our results show that the Westerlies component is primarily derived from hyper-arid deserts, whereas the EAWM-driven component originates from the semi-arid margins of East and Central Asia. Of importance is the finding that Westerly-driven transport reflects a coherent response to global cooling and hemispheric thermal gradients, whilst the Asia monsoon contribution is mediated by vegetation cover. We further demonstrate that hydroclimatic fluctuations in EAWM marginal zones modulate dust availability through vegetation-induced surface roughness and pedogenic refinement, resulting in a pronounced non-linear relationship between dust flux and wind energetics. This suggests the ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus the tropical ocean, necessitating integration of dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape interventions on dust into Earth System Models to predict global carbon cycling in a warming world. “Ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus on the tropical ocean, shown using grain size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting of a 4-million-year-long sediment record from the Philippine Sea”
research_question: How can Westerly and East Asian Winter Monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean be differentiated over the last 4 million years?
main_finding: Westerly dust originates from hyper-arid deserts and responds to global cooling, while Asian monsoon dust comes from semi-arid margins influenced by vegetation cover, showing a nonlinear relationship with wind energetics.
theme: Climate impacts of dust flux and Earth System modeling

title: An Early Jurassic soft eggshell provides insights into the evolutionary history of dinosaur eggs
authors: Zhiyong Di; Haiquan Wang; Tao Wang; Z H Dong; Xiaoli Li; Feng Zhang; Xiaoguang Li; Heyv Lv; Tianyu Ai
abstract: Early eggshell fossils offer invaluable insights into evolutionary innovations in over 300 million years of amniote egg history. However, the incompleteness of the dinosaur eggshell fossil record hinders ancestral state reconstruction and leads to uncertainty about whether the first dinosaur egg was soft-shelled, semi-rigid-shelled, or rigid-shelled. Herein, we present a fossilized soft eggshell (Mutabilisoolithus dawaensis) from an Early Jurassic basal sauropodomorph. We find that M. dawaensis has a soft, plastic-like deformation, a thick cuticle, a thin calcareous layer formed by non-interlocking shell units, and a significantly thick shell membrane. Its shell membrane is similar to that of avian eggs in structure, diameter, and arrangement of the fibers, as well as in the distinctions among outer, inner, and limiting membrane layers, but it is much thicker than that of avian eggs. In dinosaurian egg evolutionary history, M. dawaensis provides evidence of early Jurassic soft-shelled eggs, may represent the earliest stage of biomineralization, and bridges the gap between non-biomineralized membranous soft eggshells and biomineralized semi-rigid eggshells. Fossil dinosaur eggs are extremely rare, and there is uncertainty about their ancestral anatomy and evolution. A newly described Early Jurassic sauropodomorph soft-shelled egg offers valuable insights into the reproductive biology of dinosaurs.
research_question: What are the characteristics and evolutionary significance of Early Jurassic soft dinosaur eggshells?
main_finding: Discovery of a fossilized soft eggshell from an Early Jurassic basal sauropodomorph showing features bridging non-biomineralized and biomineralized eggshells.
theme: Paleontology and evolutionary biology of dinosaur eggshells

title: Programmable roll-to-roll laser processing for high value application of low-grade carbon fiber materials
authors: Guangmeng Chen; Wenjie Yu; 江广华; Li Jia; Ziqiang Hu; Weiwei Zhao; Xiaosu Yi; Xiaoqing Liu
abstract: Abstract Growing production of carbon fibers generates substantial short-chopped fibers that are difficult for high-value use due to their structural discontinuity. Carbon fiber felts offer potential, yet weak inter-fiber bonding and poor conductivity limit the performance. We report a roll‑to‑roll laser processing strategy that uses a liquid precursor to form laser‑induced graphene at fiber‑fiber interfaces, creating conductive pathways and mechanical interconnections. This approach increases tensile strength from 4.1 to 32.2 MPa and electrical conductivity from 1224.0 to 15151.5 S/m. The resulting films demonstrate efficient electrothermal de‑icing and, after copper deposition, lightning strike protection with a damage area of 9657 mm² and depth of 0.4 mm, comparable to aluminum mesh but with 15% lower weight. A custom‑built laser platform enables scalable production. Here, we show the conversion of low‑grade carbon fibers into lightweight, functional films for aerospace applications via scalable laser processing.
query: energy storage flexibility; renewable energy land use
research_question: Can roll-to-roll laser processing improve the mechanical and electrical properties of low-grade carbon fiber materials?
main_finding: Laser processing with a liquid precursor forms conductive graphene pathways, significantly enhancing tensile strength and conductivity of carbon fiber felts.
theme: Advanced materials processing for enhanced carbon fiber performance

title: Single-atom-doped zeolite electrolyte for quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries
authors: Lutong Shan; Fulong Li; Zixuan Wang; Zhenyue Xing; Shan Guo; Tsung‐Yi Chen; Wei‐Hsiang Huang; Xiaodong Shi; Xinlong Tian; Guanzhou Zhu
abstract: Quasi-solid electrolytes can mitigate polyiodide shuttling and suppress parasitic reactions at zinc negative electrode in zinc-iodine batteries by reducing free water, but their limited liquid content often results in sluggish interfacial charge transfer. Here we show liquid-electrolyte-wetted quasi-solid electrolytes by combining single-atom-modified zeolites (single-atom = iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper) with zinc sulfate aqueous solution for high-rate zinc-iodine batteries. Theoretical calculations, in situ spectroscopy, and laser confocal microscopy reveal that the single-atom metal sites enhance iodine conversion kinetics and suppress polyiodide shuttling through a synergistic catalytic-adsorption effect, with iron-doped zeolite exhibiting the strongest performance. Iron-doped zeolite further stabilizes water molecules, suppresses side reactions, and promotes uniform zinc deposition. The iron-doped zeolite-assembled zinc-iodine batteries maintain a discharge capacity of 81.2 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) after 6,800 cycles at 4 A g−1, while proof-of-concept pouch cells exhibit a capacity of 147.6 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) or 52 mAh g−1 (based on total positive electrode mass) after 200 cycles at 0.5 A g−1. Lastly, iron-doped zeolite also demonstrates compatibility with other positive electrode materials for rechargeable zinc batteries. Quasi-solid zinc iodine batteries face sluggish kinetics due to low liquid content. Here, authors report single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes that simultaneously catalyze iodine conversion, suppress polyiodide shuttling, and stabilize zinc deposition, achieving 6,800 stable cycles at high rates and demonstrating proof-of-concept pouch-cell performance.
research_question: Can single-atom-doped zeolite electrolytes improve performance and stability of quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries?
main_finding: Single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes enhance iodine conversion kinetics, suppress polyiodide shuttling, stabilize zinc deposition, and enable long cycle life at high rates.
theme: Energy storage materials and battery technology

title: Molecular insights into GPR55 modulation reveal an atypical activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent efficacy regulation
authors: Tobias Claff; Chamalee Demalgiriya-Gamage; Andhika Bintang Mahardhika; Nikolaos Angelos Stamos; Frederik Bangnowski; Xue Sun; Katharina L. Duerr; Carol V. Robinson; Rainer Haney; Lee Frego; Herbert Nar; Christa Elisabeth Müller; Rebecca Ebenhoch; Jörg Thomas Kley; Dietmar Weichert
abstract: GPR55 is a lipid-activated G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) implicated in metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) species are proposed as endogenous agonists, but progress in understanding GPR55 function has still been limited by suboptimal chemical probes. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GPR55 in both inactive and active states. The inactive-state structure bound to the inverse agonist CID16020046 facilitated the rational design of an improved in vitro tool compound, BI-8310. Surprisingly, mutation of a glycosylation site in extracellular loop 2 converted CID16020046 into a potent agonist, enabling co-structure determination of the active, G13-bound receptor. Comparative analysis of both states bound to the same ligand provides insights into an atypical activation mechanism that diverges from the typical helix VI outward movement observed in other GPCRs. Functional mutagenesis, N-glycoproteomics, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) substantiate the findings. These results establish a basis for targeted modulation of GPR55 in pathophysiological conditions. GPR55 is a lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor. Here, authors present cryo-EM structures of inactive and active states of GPR55, revealing an atypical activation mechanism with a glycosylation-dependent switch in ligand efficacy.
research_question: How does GPR55 activation and glycosylation regulate ligand efficacy at the molecular level?
main_finding: Cryo-EM structures reveal an atypical GPR55 activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent switch converting an inverse agonist into a potent agonist.
theme: Molecular pharmacology of GPCR activation

title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
authors: Kyle Davis; Joanna Tannous
abstract: Abstract Over the past two decades, there has been a staggering increase in greenhouse gas emissions, particularly carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from unrestrained anthropogenic activities, leading to notable environmental shifts. Despite continuous efforts to reduce emissions, the world is not making satisfactory progress, which calls for immediate action to implement alternative strategies to enhance environmental sustainability. The Earth naturally absorbs and stores carbon through various processes, but merely keeping pace with ongoing human activities is no longer sufficient. Land plants and marine prokaryotes absorb CO 2 during photosynthesis and store carbon as biomass. Eukaryotic organisms also represent a valuable resource that can provide insights into the biological fixation and removal of atmospheric CO 2 . Expanding the capacities of Earth’s natural systems offers enormous potential for enhancing carbon sinks and promoting environmental resilience. Although extensive synthetic engineering of plant systems has been conducted to enhance their native carbon fixation pathways, research on microorganisms, especially fungi, has been limited. In this review, we specifically explore the role of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, elucidating their responses to environmental shifts and their potential for climate change mitigation. We place particular emphasis on the role of various fungal guilds in this process, highlighting those that should be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications. We then engage with previous endeavors to address primary challenges in advancing genetic tools for these understudied fungi. Lastly, we discuss how integrating synthetic biology practices into the field of soil-associated fungi can drive advances in long-term carbon storage, enhance degradation of environmental pollutants, and improve nutrient exchange and soil health, contributing to more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions. Rising carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are driving environmental change and increasing the need for strategies that strengthen natural carbon sinks and ecosystem resilience. While plants and microorganisms play important roles in carbon capture and storage, the potential of soil-associated fungi remains comparatively underexplored, particularly from a synthetic biology perspective. In this Review, we examine the roles of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, their responses to environmental change, and their potential contributions to climate change mitigation. We highlight key fungal guilds that could be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications and discuss current challenges in developing genetic tools for understudied fungi. Finally, we explore how engineering soil-associated fungi could support long-term carbon storage while providing broader environmental benefits, including pollutant degradation, nutrient exchange, and improved soil health. Together, these opportunities position fungal synthetic biology as a promising approach for developing more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions.

title: Exsolution of metal nanoparticles by control of point defects
authors: Andreas Rosnes; Bo Jiang; Holger von Wenckstern; Øystein Prytz; Jonathan M. Polfus
abstract: Abstract Exsolution involves redox precipitation of metal nanoparticles from metal oxides, resulting in materials that exhibit excellent electrocatalytic properties and hold great promise for novel types of nanoscale heterostructures. However, a coherent understanding of the phenomenon is lacking. Here, exsolution is described by three point defect equations involving the reduction of the host oxide, reduction and exsolution of the transition metal, and annihilation of host unit cells. Guided by their predictions, significantly enhanced exsolution in terms of molar amount, rate, and nucleation density is achieved by acceptor substitution in the system La 0.2 Ca 0.7 Ti 0.95 Cu 0.05 O 3− δ , as shown by atomic scale imaging and in situ X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy. It is demonstrated that the oxygen stoichiometry of the parent oxide increases upon exsolution despite oxygen loss in the reducing environment. Furthermore, strain in both the host oxide and the exsolved metal can constitute an additional thermodynamic barrier for exsolution beyond the availability of the required point defects.

title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states
authors: Alina Vo Vo; Yuan-En Sun; Justin G. English; Michael J. Robertson
abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based ensemble prediction we can reliably design fiducial markers to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights major gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformations. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins. Visualizing how drugs reshape GPCR receptors by cryo-EM has been difficult for many conformational states. Here, authors use designed protein fiducials to image elusive GPCR states, revealing details of ligand induced receptor activation.

title: Coupled sea-level and biodiversity dynamics during the Cambrian SPICE event
authors: Meng Wang; Yukun Shi; Aihua Yang; Haotian Zhang; Xiaoyu Zhang; Yujing Wu; yujie shi; Jianbo Liu; Ren Wei; Zhijun Jin; Mingsong Li
abstract: The prominent Cambrian Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion (SPICE) stands as one of Earth’s largest carbon cycle perturbations, marked by widespread marine anoxia, climatic upheaval, and biotic turnover, yet the complete extent and interplay of these environmental changes remain unclear. Here, we integrate high-resolution astrochronology, carbonate carbon isotope records from the North China Block and marine species richness to investigate sedimentary and biogeochemical responses during the SPICE interval. Time series analysis reveals a distinct ~2-million-year sedimentary rhythm that aligns with cycles in reconstructed sea-level fluctuations and biodiversity dynamics. We show that sea-level changes preceded shifts in benthic species richness by 70 kyr, linking astronomically paced eustatic oscillations to marine redox fluctuations and concurrent biodiversity turnover. These findings establish pivotal constraints on ocean-climate interactions during this critical interval, elucidating Earth system resilience to extreme climatic and biogeochemical perturbations. Using astrochronology, Wang et al. estimate that relative sea-level change led benthic turnover by ~70,000 years during the late Cambrian SPICE event under their age model, supporting links among orbital forcing, marine anoxia and biodiversity loss.

title: An integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture with Cu dual active-sites for all-solid-state Li–CO2 batteries
authors: Yunyun Xu; Dashuai Wang; Yuejiao Li; Haifeng Qi; Zhuobin Guo; Tasmia Azam; Pratteek Das; Zhong‐Shuai Wu; Hui–Ming Cheng
abstract: All-solid-state Li–CO2 batteries are limited by sluggish interfacial CO2 redox kinetics and the incomplete decomposition of insulating Li2CO3 at rigid solid-solid-gas interfaces. Here, we report an integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture in which copper atomic clusters and single atoms are co-anchored on freestanding N-doped carbon nanotubes and coupled with a succinonitrile/Li1+xAlyGe2-y(PO4)3-based solid-state electrolyte. The conformal ion-conducting phase and conductive nanotube scaffold provide coupled pathways for Li+, electrons and CO2 at the cathode interface. Electronic coupling between the copper atomic clusters and single atoms induces charge transfer from the former to the latter (~0.457 e−), rendering the Cu cluster sites partially cationic and facilitating the activation of carbonate intermediates. This dual-site configuration changes the discharge pathway and lowers the reaction energy of the rate-determining step to 2.412 eV. The assembled battery delivers a discharge capacity of 21356 mAh g−1 at 200 mA g−1 and operates for 260 cycles (>1000 h) at 500 mA g−1 with an energy efficiency of 78%. This work provides an interfacial design strategy for solid-state Li–CO2 batteries by coupling continuous transport pathways with electronically regulated dual Cu active sites. Stimuli responsive assemblies can offer precise control over behaviour, but use of gases for this control is rare. Here, the authors report the use of carbon dioxide for tuneable nanoparticle response, directed by changes in peptide structure.

title: A synaptic mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission
authors: Fenglan Wang; Wenna Zhao; Xin Lin; Xiaotian Bian; Qingwen Yang; Zhongqun Chen; Fang He; Xiaoqing Liu; Yu Xi; Bilin Rao; Jun Cao; Jun Zhang; Jia Qu
abstract: Photoreceptor synapses rely on mitochondria, synaptic ribbons, and vesicles, yet how these elements integrate into functional units remains unclear. Here we show, using focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and electrophysiology, that they form synaptic mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complexes (sMRVcs) with fundamentally different architectures in rods and cones. Rod spherules exhibit a strict 1:1 pairing of a single megamitochondrion with one ribbon, sustaining continuous glutamate release in darkness, whereas cone pedicles contain multiple distributed sMRVcs. Disrupting the mitochondrial anchor protein syntaphilin shifts this ratio to 2:1 in rods, with additional mitochondria recruited near the ribbon, and enhances synaptic transmission. In a retinal degeneration model, the sMRVc progressively disassembles before functional decline, with fragmented mitochondria, detached ribbons, and dispersed vesicles. We also identify non-ribbon release sites selectively targeting horizontal cells. These findings establish the sMRVc as a conserved structural–metabolic module whose subtype-specific organization reflects distinct visual demands and whose integrity is essential for synaptic health. Researchers find photoreceptor synapses contain mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complexes: rods have a 1:1 megamitochondrion–ribbon pair; cones have distributed units. Disrupting mitochondrial anchoring shifts rods to 2:1 and boosts signaling, while degeneration breaks the complex apart.

title: ZEB1 maintains energy metabolism to sustain cardiac function through synergistic regulation with TEAD1
authors: Taiwei Chen; Zhinan Wu; Fei Liao; Yiwen Shen; Zhimin Wang; Yuxuan Qian; Guqing Luo; Wenyi Xu; Xinjie He; Yue Huang; Jiyuan Chen; Bihe Xu; Song Z. Ding; Jun Pu
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in heart failure (HF), but its regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1), a transcription factor initially identified as a regulator of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, has recently been implicated in metabolic regulation. Here, we show that ZEB1 expression is reduced in failing cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Zeb1 leads to progressive HF with impaired glycolysis and fatty acid metabolism. Mechanistically, ZEB1 interacts with TEA domain transcription factor 1 (TEAD1) to activate metabolic genes, including pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme 1 (PKM1) and acetyl-CoA acyltransferase 2 (ACAA2), which regulate glycolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation, respectively. Loss of Acaa2 aggravates stress-induced cardiac hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. Acetate supplementation restores cardiac function in Zeb1-deficient mice, whereas ZEB1 overexpression improves pressure overload- and doxorubicin-induced HF. These findings identify the ZEB1-TEAD1 axis as a regulator of cardiac metabolic homeostasis and a potential therapeutic target for HF. Heart failure is a major health challenge, and the mechanisms driving metabolic dysfunction in the failing heart remain poorly understood. Here, the authors show that ZEB1-TEAD1 signaling preserves cardiac energy metabolism and that restoring ZEB1 or supplementing its downstream metabolite acetate mitigates heart failure progression.

title: Scalable architecture for measurement-induced squeezed light interferometers
authors: Abhinav Verma; Jacob Hastrup; Jonas Schou Neergaard-Nielsen; Ulrik L. Andersen
abstract: Scalable interferometers lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, but their expansion has been fundamentally limited by optical losses that grow with circuit depth. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a measurement-induced architecture for multimode squeezed-light interferometers that overcomes this barrier. By shifting complexity from deep optical networks to programmable homodyne measurements, we realize effective transformations within a shallow, low-loss platform. We validate the principle with a six-mode device and extend it to a 400-mode interferometer, marking a leap in scale beyond conventional designs. Crucially, this strategy not only enables scalable squeezed light interferometry but also provides a powerful route to the generation of large-scale entangled states-a key requirement for quantum computing, simulation, and communication. Our results establish measurement-induced circuits as a practical pathway toward noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) applications and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.
research_question: How can scalable multimode squeezed-light interferometers be realized to overcome optical loss limitations?
main_finding: A measurement-induced architecture shifts complexity to programmable homodyne measurements, enabling scalable, low-loss squeezed-light interferometers demonstrated up to 400 modes.
theme: Quantum photonic technologies and scalable interferometry

title: Representing canopy interception in a distributed snow model to improve snow accumulation and melt timing
authors: Yijing Liu; J. Michelle Hu; Alvaro Robledano; S. McKenzie Skiles
abstract: Seasonal snowmelt is a vital water resource for downstream populations and supports ecological processes in the mountainous Western United States. In subalpine forests, snow interception by tree canopies strongly influences snow accumulation, snow duration, and runoff timing. However, canopy interception has not been incorporated into the widely used, process-based distributed snow energy balance model, iSnobal. To address this gap, we integrated multiple forest canopy snow processes into iSnobal. To assess the version of iSnobal with canopy processes, it was run over five water years in the East River Watershed, a mountainous, partially forested basin in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Across model runs, 50–––150 mm of snowfall, equivalent to 10% − 30% of cumulative snowfall, was intercepted annually. Within the canopy, melt dominated snow loss, while wind-driven unloading was limited and elevation-dependent. Relative to baseline runs, snow depths were decreased (mean 0.09–0.11 m) and snow cover duration was shortened (7–16 days) due to delayed snow onset and faster snow depletion. The model was assessed against lidar-mapped snow depth, which showed that accounting for interception improved model performance, with 39.4% to 57.3% of pixels exhibiting better agreement and reduced errors, especially during late melt (May and June). Random forest analysis identified intercepted snowfall, snow onset date, leaf area index, cumulative snowfall, and aspect as primary controls on snow depth differences between default iSnobal and its canopy-enabled version. This study emphasizes the importance of accounting for forest canopy processes in snow models and provides a basis for more reliable snowmelt inputs to water supply forecasting in snow-dominated forested regions.
research_question: How does incorporating canopy interception processes into a distributed snow model affect snow accumulation and melt timing?
main_finding: Including canopy interception in the iSnobal model improved snow depth predictions and better captured snow cover duration and melt timing.
theme: Hydrological modeling of snow processes with forest canopy effects

title: Persistent seasonal deoxygenation alters benthic metabolic processes and accelerates hypoxia feedbacks in the Baltic Sea
authors: Shuba Varshini Alampalli; Stefanie Böhnke-Brandt; Nicole Adam-Beyer; Katja Laufer; Klaus Wallmann; Hermann W. Bange; Helmke Hepach; Matthias Thiele; Florian Scholz; Emanuel Wyler; M Landthaler; Isabel Diercks; Janina Fuß; Mirjam Perner
abstract: Abstract Nutrient enrichment and warming cause widespread costal deoxygenation, leading to hypoxia or even anoxia in bottom waters. The benthic-water-column-feedbacks that develop under persistent seasonal oxygen depletion and amplify hypoxia remain poorly constrained. A 15-month study of a seasonally hypoxic to anoxic costal system in the southwestern Baltic Sea combined water-column monitoring, sediment chemistry, metabolic rates and microbial analyses with historic data to reveal pronounced seasonal shifts in sediment processes. During winter oxygenation, organic matter degradation, fermentation, aerobic respiration, nitrate- and iron-reduction and microbial competition increased. Re-ventilation following anoxia did not reset sediment biogeochemistry, but initiated intensified oxygen consumption, microbial biosynthetic activity and anaerobic carbon re-cycling. Reactive ironoxyhydroxides became exhausted, the sulfidic zone shoaled and sulfate reduction and pyrite formation rates increased through fall. These processes reinforced benthic feedbacks, progressively reducing the sediment’s capacity to retain sulfide over years. This weakening of sedimentary resilience exacerbates sulfide accumulation in eutrophic costal environments with growing chances of sulfidic deep-water upwelling.

title: Multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor for real-time blood monitoring
authors: Zhizhi Wu; Fan Chen; Jiaheng Liang; Yufei Zhang; Qiyao Huang; Chi Zhang; Peng Li; Shoujie Li; Haihua Shu; Xin Cheng; Hwa‐Yaw Tam; Yunfei Chai; Zijian Zheng
abstract: Accurate and real-time monitoring of blood electrolyte composition, particularly sodium (Na + ) and potassium (K + ), is crucial for guiding intraoperative and postoperative decisions, as these ions regulate critical bodily functions such as cardiac rhythm and fluid balance. Current blood analysis relies on ex vivo blood sampling, which introduces substantial time delays and can be susceptible to inaccuracies caused by temperature fluctuations. To address these challenges, we report here a multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor (MIFS) capable of monitoring Na + and K + ions in real time directly in the bloodstream. MIFS integrates three parallel liquid metal channels with a multilayer surface-electrode architecture, which synergistically enhances sensitivity, minimizes sensing drift, ensures mechanical flexibility, and offers outstanding biocompatibility for vascular implantation. In vivo testing in rabbit models and validation in human blood samples demonstrate MIFS’s superior sensing accuracy, real-time, and stable sensing in agreement with conventional ex vivo measurements. This work paves the way for real-time blood monitoring in clinical practice.
research_question: Can a multiplexed implantable fiber sensor enable real-time monitoring of blood sodium and potassium levels?
main_finding: The developed sensor accurately and stably monitors Na+ and K+ ions in real time within the bloodstream.
theme: Biomedical sensing technology

title: Integrating a global glacier model into local hydrological modeling: Impacts on melt contributions
authors: Justine Berg; Pascal Horton; Martina Kauzlaric; Alexandra von der Esch; Bettina Schaefli
abstract: Abstract. Snow and glacier meltwater are critical water resources for mountain regions, yet their accurate representation in hydrological models remains challenging. As climate change alters the timing and magnitude of melt contributions, accurate partitioning between snow and glacier sources becomes increasingly important. To address this challenge, this study couples the hydrological model HBV (as implemented in the Raven modeling framework) with the Global Glacier Evolution Model GloGEM and integrates a snow redistribution scheme for application across 14 glaciated headwater catchments in Switzerland. At this local catchment scale, we investigate whether glacier constraints and the addition of snow redistribution reduce parameter equifinality and increase the reliability of melt contribution estimates. Simulations are evaluated against observed streamflow, gridded snow water equivalent data, and glacier melt data based on observed mass balance. The gravitational snow redistribution algorithm successfully prevents unrealistic high-elevation snow accumulation and improves catchment average SWE simulation performance. Uncoupled HBV configurations outperform coupled HBV-GloGEM setups according to streamflow metrics. However, this superior performance is achieved by simulating glacier melt rates exceeding GloGEM estimates and glacier storage change data by factors of 2–3 in some catchments, effectively using glacier ice to offset precipitation biases in forcing data, which can be critical for climate change impact studies. Glacier melt contributions can vary by nearly an order of magnitude among best-performing parameter sets, highlighting severe parameter equifinality. Coupling with GloGEM, calibrated using glacier-specific geodetic mass balance, produces glacier melt consistent with observations and substantially improves identifiability of both glacier and snowmelt contributions. Despite lower streamflow performance metrics, glacier melt constraints prevent compensatory errors that would compromise projections as melt dynamics shift under climate change. Applying this framework to future climate scenarios and integrating additional constraints such as snow observations may further improve the reliability of melt contribution projections.
research_question: Does coupling a global glacier model with local hydrological modeling improve accuracy of meltwater source partitioning?
main_finding: Coupling HBV with GloGEM improves glacier melt estimates and reduces parameter equifinality despite lower streamflow performance.
theme: Hydrological modeling of glacier and snow melt contributions under climate change

title: Hemolymph pressure-mediated friction in the tarsus of the desert locust ( Schistocerca gregaria )
authors: Jiahui Zhao; Jian Chen; Stanislav N. Gorb; Chuchu Li
abstract: ) performs high-acceleration jumps within milliseconds, relying not only on powerful muscles and spring-loaded hindlegs, but also on precise tarsi-substrate interactions. Although the mechanics of jumping have been extensively studied, the mechanisms enabling rapid attachment and detachment remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the frictional properties of hindleg tarsi under controlled low-speed contact conditions targeting selected loading features associated with jumping. We hypothesize that locusts coordinate tarsal cuticular structures with internal hemolymph pressure to modulate contact mechanics. Using high-speed videography, a suite of advanced microscopic techniques, biomechanical experiments, and biomimetic prototypes, we provide evidence that hemolymph pressure modulates tarsal stiffness and acts together with structural asymmetry to produce direction-dependent frictional responses. This interplay may contribute to adaptive friction tuning associated with jumping. Our findings advance the understanding of locust locomotor biomechanics and suggest design principles for robotic systems requiring rapid and controllable surface engagement.

title: Gradient-interlayer–based flexible pressure sensors for high-performance robotic perception
authors: Mingyuan Sun; G L; Shuai Dong; Erlong Wang; Shi‐Yang Tang; Xuanhan Chen; Yipu Guo; Xiaoqin Sun; Xiangpeng Li; Weihua Li; Shiwu Zhang
abstract: Tactile perception systems based on flexible pressure sensors are indispensable for humanoid robots to perform dexterous manipulation, compliant interaction, and operation in visually challenging environments. Although strategies relying on surface or spatial microstructure engineering have improved sensor performance, the long-standing trade-off among sensitivity, sensing range, and linearity continues to hinder their practical deployment. Inspired by the gradient distribution of mechanoreceptors in human fingertip skin, we report a gradient-interlayer–based flexible iontronic pressure sensor (GriFIPS) in which a single direct-ink-written elastomeric mesh-like interlayer, with a centrifugal increase in aperture size, is placed between the soft electrode and an ionic hydrogel layer. Operating upstream of the functional layer, the mesh enables progressive, stage-wise contact under increasing load and decouples macroscopic contact-area evolution from the microscopic interfacial response. The sensor simultaneously achieves a sensitivity of 175.9 kPa −1 , a linear sensing range up to 360 kPa with a coefficient of determination of 0.997, a low detection limit of about 2.1 Pa, and a response time of about 25 ms, while remaining stable over 6000 loading cycles and 2000 cycles of 50% tensile strain. Building on this single-channel device, we further extend the architecture into a 3-axis gradient-interlayer–based flexible iontronic force sensor (3-axis GriFIFS) capable of resolving triaxial forces and surface textures. When integrated onto a dexterous robotic hand and combined with a temporal convolutional network, the sensors support tactile object recognition, fabric texture discrimination, human–robot interaction, and tactile-guided assembly, offering a generalizable route to tactile sensing for embodied intelligence.

title: Coupled responses of aboveground and belowground net primary productivity stability to nitrogen deposition in grasslands
authors: yaodan zhang; Siyuan Gao; Xinxin Wang; Huiying Liu
abstract: Abstract The temporal stability of plant net primary productivity (NPP), defined as the ratio of temporal mean productivity to its standard deviation, is crucial for sustaining ecosystem services. Yet, little is known about whether the effects of nitrogen deposition on aboveground NPP (ANPP) stability are coupled with corresponding changes in belowground systems. Here we conducted a global meta-analysis based on 542 multi-year observations from 111 studies to assess the impacts of nitrogen deposition on the stability of ANPP and belowground NPP (BNPP). Nitrogen addition significantly decreased the stability of both ANPP and BNPP in a synchronized manner, reflecting a coupled response resulting from the allocation trade-off between mean ANPP and BNPP and their synchronized increase in variability. Further analysis showed that the declines in both ANPP and BNPP stability were associated with decreased plant species richness under nitrogen addition. Moreover, the negative responses intensified with longer treatment durations and higher nitrogen addition intensity. These findings highlight the importance of considering above- and below-ground interactions in future ecosystem management strategies under global change scenarios.

title: Climate-driven water stress in the United States is seasonal, regional, and shaped by adaptation
authors: Joey Blumberg; Travis Warziniack
abstract: This study quantifies drivers of water use across the food-energy-water nexus and assesses how climate change, population growth, and adaptation may reshape future water scarcity in the United States. Using high frequency water withdrawal data from 2000–2020, we disentangle the effects of climate, hydrology, and socioeconomic factors on public water use, crop irrigation, and cooling for thermoelectric power generation. Future water demands (2040–2070) are estimated using recent climate and socioeconomic projections, representing 1.0 ∘C to 2.9 ∘C warming and population growth ranging from 1% to 44%. Across 28 scenarios, we estimate annual water use changes ranging from -10.7% to +28.9% for public use, +32.1% to +43.6% for crop irrigation, and -27.9% to -19.9% for thermoelectric power cooling, contingent on continued adaptive efforts. Results reveal strong sectoral variation in climate sensitivity, seasonal mismatches between water supply and demand, and shifts in regional water stress under future warming. Climate change and economic activity are reshaping when and where water stress occurs in the United States. This study identifies the drivers and locations of water stress and shows how targeted water management policies can reduce future scarcity.
