title: The need for uncertainty: why probabilistic LSTMs are key to improving flood predictions and enabling learned warning rules
authors: Sanika Baste; Sebastian Lerch; Daniel Klotz; Ralf Loritz
abstract: Abstract. Deterministic model predictions can struggle to adequately capture extreme events such as floods and droughts, which are of particular relevance in hydrology. This limitation arises because deterministic models collapse the conditional runoff distribution to a single point estimate. Probabilistic modeling provides a way to address this issue by explicitly representing uncertainty and assigning non-zero probabilities to a range of possible outcomes, including rare and extreme events, thereby capturing the full range of plausible hydrological responses. Motivated by this perspective, we examine whether probabilistic Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models improve the representation of extreme events in rainfall–-runoff simulations across Switzerland. Overall, the probabilistic models show good calibration, although some miscalibration remains for the extremes. Differences between models mainly manifest in how uncertainty is distributed: some approaches produce narrower and lighter-tailed distributions, while others yield broader distributions with heavier tails. These trade-offs highlight that probabilistic models differ not only in sharpness but also in how their calibration for rare events. We observe this tradeoff also in models' accuracy metrics. When evaluating the mean of the probabilistic predictions using the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), none of the probabilistic approaches outperform the deterministic LSTM in terms of average predictive accuracy. However, a clear advantage over the determinsitc models emerges when focusing on the tail of the discharge distribution. For the most extreme events (top 0.1 % of the discharge distribution), the deterministic LSTM underestimates more than 90 % of observed values (since it provides estimates of an expectation), whereas probabilistic predictions can capture a substantially larger fraction (67 %) of these extremes within their upper predictive bounds. Building on the additional information provided by probabilistic runoff predictions, we further show how they can be translated into actionable flood warnings using reinforcement learning. To this end, we introduce a Flood Risk Communication Agent (FRiCA) that operates on probabilistic runoff predictions and learns decision rules for issuing warnings of varying intensity. The FRiCA is implemented as an LSTM-based policy network and is trained by rewarding correct warning levels while penalizing the underestimation of flood severity. Results indicate that the FRiCA outperforms simple fixed heuristics, such as issuing warnings based on the predictive mean or a fixed high quantile (e.g., the 99th percentile). While this behavior already demonstrates the potential of reinforcement learning for improved flood risk communication, it also motivates further exploration of better reward design and policy network definition for context-dependent decision policies that adapt to varying hydrological and societal contexts.

title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
authors: Jenny U. Tran; Thyandra A. Martinez; Christopher P. Jurich; Margaret R. Josling; Julian M. Zhang; Pedro H Ayres-Galhardo; Jens Meiler; Zhongyue John Yang; Jason A. MacGurn; Breann L. Brown
abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

title: S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine triggers an adaptive response that extends lifespan through the YBT1 ABC transporter
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: Koji Masumura; S. Kawasaki; Mayu Tsutsumi; Hiiro Yamashita; Muneyoshi Kanai; Haruto Nakajo; Wakaba Yagi; Shoma Katsunoi; Kaori Yoneyama; Miyuki Kawano‐Kawada; Takayuki Sekito; Takafumi Ogawa; Tomoyoshi Soga; Masaki Mizunuma
abstract: S -adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is a fundamental methyl donor; however, the physiological role of its byproduct and competitive inhibitor, S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH), remains unclear. Here, we show that transient reactive oxygen species (ROS) production triggered by SAH during the early logarithmic phase mimics partial SAH hydrolase inhibition, extending the yeast chronological lifespan (CLS) through a hormetic mechanism. This study reveals that the dual nature of ROS in aging is determined by the specific degree of SAH hydrolase activity. We identified the adenosine 5’-triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporter Ybt1 as a key downstream effector of SAH. Ybt1 localizes to the vacuolar membrane and facilitates the sequestration of SAM from the cytosol into the vacuole. Notably, YBT1 overexpression extends CLS, mimicking SAH effects through an integrated pathway involving target of rapamycin complex 1 downregulation, autophagy, and adenosine 5’-monophosphate-activated protein kinase activation. Our findings establish that SAH acts as a metabolic signal coupling nutrient and energy availability to longevity via Ybt1, defining an adaptive/hormetic response for lifespan regulation in yeast.

title: Regenerable, closed-loop, nonenzymatic continuous glucose monitoring enabled by in situ electrochemical interfacial alkalinization
authors: Qiang Zeng; Liangjun Xia; Junyao Gong; Jieyao Qin; Sijie Zhou; FU Zhuan; Jiajing Zhang; Ke Lin; Chunhua Zhang; Wei Zhang; Weilin Xu
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring in interstitial fluid (ISF) is important for diabetes management, but enzyme-based sensors can lose activity, while many nonenzymatic alternatives show optimal activity in alkaline media. Here we present a regenerable wrist-worn hollow microneedle platform for closed-loop nonenzymatic ISF glucose monitoring. Negative pressure extracts ISF into a detachable sensor cartridge that separates the tissue interface from the electrochemical sensing chamber and enables rinsing and reuse. A brief cathodic step triggers the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at an Au–Pt/Ni foam electrode, electrochemically generating a local alkaline interface for the subsequent glucose oxidation reaction (GOR). Integrated pH feedback regulates the HER–GOR sequence. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate rapid ISF extraction and quasi-continuous glucose monitoring in rats, with preliminary feasibility in one human participant. This work illustrates local microenvironment regulation as a strategy for enabling alkaline-dependent glucose electrocatalysis in near-neutral ISF. Continuous glucose monitoring is central to diabetes management, yet conventional testing provides only intermittent snapshots and may miss clinically important glycaemic fluctuations. Here, the authors present a wrist-worn hollow microneedle platform that combines active interstitial fluid extraction with nonenzymatic electrochemical glucose sensing in a wearable format. Its detachable microneedle cartridge enables independent cleaning or replacement, supporting quasi-continuous monitoring while improving practicality and long-term usability for wearable glucose tracking.

title: Polymer Brush-Mediated Surface-Initiated Polycondensation Enables sp2C-COF Thin Films with Controlled Crystallinity and High Photocatalytic Performance
authors: Lingjie He; Wuxin Zhang; Yuxiang Zhao; 傅关根; Ling Yin; Wenkai Zhao; Mengwei Chen; Jun Yong He; Liping Wang; Tao Zhang
abstract: Sp2-carbon-conjugated covalent organic frameworks (sp2C-COFs) hold exceptional potential as π-conjugated semiconductors for optoelectronics and photocatalysis, yet their thin-film fabrication suffers from irreversible C = C linkages that impede crystallinity and morphology control. Herein, we report a polymer brush-mediated surface-initiated polycondensation (PB-SIP) strategy to synthesize the sp2C-COF films with controlled crystallinity and morphology. The polymer brush layer acts as both a surface-tethered initiator and a soft interfacial regulator, enabling precise control over nucleation and crystallization kinetics. By modulating the polymer brush thickness, we achieve sp2C-COF films with enhanced crystallinity and reduced surface roughness. Notably, this method allows the growth of highly crystalline, homogeneous sp2C-COF coatings on 3D porous sponges, which exhibit near-complete photocatalytic antibacterial efficiency (99.4%) in natural sewage under visible light. This interfacial engineering paradigm advances the rational design of crystalline sp2C-COF films for energy-environment applications. Conjugated covalent organic frameworks (COF) hold exceptional potential as semiconductors for optoelectronics and photocatalysis, but control over crystallinity and morphology remains challenging. Here the authors report a polymer brush- mediated surface-initiated polycondensation strategy to synthesize the conjugated COF films with controlled crystallinity and morphology.

title: One Health in action: regional innovations and shared challenges in addressing antimicrobial resistance
authors: Godwin Pius Ohemu; Adam Dale; Babafela Awosile; Robert Fraser Terry; Kiplangat Sigei; Anuj Sharma; Geetanjali Kapoor; Tine Rikke Jørgensen; Mohammed Alkhaldi; Mohamed Elhadidy; Heba Mahrous; Shaffi Fazaludeen Koya; Said Abukhattab; Maryam Wakkaf; Kome Otokunefor
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries, yet perspectives and innovations from these regions remain underrepresented. During World Antimicrobial Awareness Week 2025, the AMR Knowledge Hub convened a four-day webinar series on AMR challenges and One Health solutions across three regions, with a country spotlight on Nigeria. Discussions highlight critical gaps in political commitment, sustainable financing, and locally relevant evidence, particularly on antibiotic stewardship. Regional and country experiences demonstrate the importance of context-specific research, locally driven innovation, and stronger governance. Integrating these voices into global AMR governance is essential for a more equitable, effective, and enduring response. Authors present their work on practitioner perspectives on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from Africa, Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa, with a country spotlight on Nigeria, highlighting shared implementation gaps and locally driven innovations.

title: Multifunctional submicron-scale porous water-foamed cementitious materials
authors: Guangqi Xiong; Zhao Meng; Yanran Cheng; Shuangshuang Liu; Yong Zheng; Chi Sun Poon; Shipeng Zhang
abstract: Abstract Conventional cement-based materials face a fundamental trade-off between low density and high performance, owing to their limited ability to precisely control pore structure. We use ultrasound carbonation to tailor the water distribution and confinement within the flocculation structure, thereby directing product nucleation and growth, and ultimately yielding a multifunctional submicron-scale water-foamed cementitious material. The matrix exhibits a highly refined pore network, 96.8% of which is smaller than 200 nm. The specific compressive strength is 22.5 kN·m·kg −1 , representing an increase of up to 162% relative to a laboratory-prepared foamed concrete control. Simultaneously, the sound transmission loss increases by 131.8% and 107.0% at 2000 Hz and 4000 Hz, respectively, while cumulative CO 2 uptake reaches 7.11% per unit mass of cement after 28 days. The approach relies solely on cement and water as raw materials, reducing process complexity and showing potential for production.

title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces
authors: Ran Huo; Shengyun Huang; Dixiang Gong; Xin Zhou; Heng Zhu; Pengyun Zhang; Hideaki Okuyama; Guangyu Bao; Xuan Li; Aram Bahmani; Lisa Martignetti; Zixin Zhang; Hongyu Hou; Changhong Cao; Yixun Cheng
abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
authors: Xiao Xiao; Chang Liu; Zimo Wang; Xiao Xiao; He Wang; Chengyue Lu; Xiao Li; Junyi Yin; Xiao Li; Wei Zhang; Gang Ge; Wenbo Ding; Guangmin Zhou; Patrick Chia; Lei Shen
abstract: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization-problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy
authors: Feiyao Yang; Yu Tian; Enyi Zhang; Lixue Yang; Ziyue You; Puguang Peng; Qian Han; Yan Du; Haiwei Li; Yongquan Wu; Houfang Liu; Anfu Zhou; Tian‐Ling Ren; Weiping Sun; Zhong Lin Wang
abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

title: Life-Cycle Burden Shifting in Solvent-Based Regeneration of PFOS-Laden Granular Activated Carbon
authors: Yue Pang; Hao Guan; Wentian Zheng; jiayi Yuan; Runzhi Wang; Yumeng Zhao; Yifei Wang; Meng Sun
abstract: Granular activated carbon (GAC) is widely used to remove perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) from contaminated water, yet its sustainable regeneration remains challenging. Solvent-based regeneration preserves the carbon matrix but may shift environmental burdens toward solvent production, chemical use, energy demand, and downstream waste management. Here we present a life cycle assessment (LCA) of PFOS-laden GAC regeneration using deionized water (GAC-WR) and ethanol (GAC-ER). We identify electricity-driven elution and downstream incineration as the dominant environmental hotspots across 18 midpoint impact categories. Selected chemical-assisted configurations (NaOH-modified water and HCl-modified ethanol) improved regeneration efficiency and reduced environmental impacts under the evaluated conditions by reducing virgin GAC supplementation. An industrial-scale model incorporating equipment upscaling and thermal integration further mitigated laboratory-specific energy overestimation. Compared with the corresponding baseline scenarios using the global electricity mix, hydropower-based electricity reduces global warming potential to 3.30 and 8.26 kg CO2e kg-1 for GAC-WR and GAC-ER, respectively, while increasing life-cycle water consumption to 230% and 266% of the respective baselines. This cross-category burden shift demonstrates that reducing climate impacts does not necessarily reduce the broader life-cycle environmental footprint. Overall, sustainable solvent-based GAC regeneration requires balancing regeneration efficiency, energy supply, chemical inputs, solvent recovery, and management of PFAS-containing wastes.

title: Insights from coproduced scenarios toward urban sustainability transformations
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: David M. Iwaniec; Nancy B. Grimm; Marta Berbés Blázquez; Elizabeth M. Cook; Tischa A. Muñoz‐Erickson; The UREx City Scenarios Team
abstract: Urban sustainability transformations call for fundamental shifts in how cities are organized, developed, and governed. Yet we need a better understanding of the diversity of visions and pathways that can enable transformative change. We address this gap through an analysis of 60 coproduced positive scenario visions and pathways developed using the Sustainable Future Scenario process, across nine US and Latin American cities participating in the Urban Resilience to Extremes Sustainability Research Network. We engaged diverse urban stakeholders-including government, nonprofit, and private decision-makers, community leaders, residents, and academic collaborators-in more than 20 coproduction workshops to explore alternative urban futures of sustainability and resilience. We examined how the coproduced scenarios represent five domains of transformative change (nature-human relationships, economic transformation, governance, social and environmental justice, and infrastructure futures) and four theories of transformative change (structural/institutional, agency/power, goals of the system, and worldviews/values). Most pathways combined multiple theories of change operating across multiple domains, revealing urban transformations as entangled rather than singular interventions. Some strategies were common across cities-car-free regions, decentralized infrastructure, community-based governance, expanded fundamental rights-yet were pursued with different transformative aims, demonstrating how a strategy's transformative intent depends on the theories of change behind it. These findings position coproduced scenarios as more than a normative or planning tool and offer an analytical approach for surfacing the possibility space of urban transformation.

title: ICU-acquired pneumonia beyond pathogen detection
authors: Ignacio Martín‐Loeches; Antoni Torres
abstract: Intensive care unit-acquired pneumonia is often treated as a binary diagnosis, although clinical deterioration, imaging and microbial detection describe different aspects of disease. This Perspective proposes an explicit, graded and revisable assessment of whether a detected organism plausibly causes the current lung injury. The framework encompasses pneumonia arising during ventilation, pneumonia that precedes intubation and pneumonia in non-ventilated ICU patients. It places molecular results within clinical, anatomical, microbiological and host context and uses formal reassessment at 48–72 hours to guide treatment continuation, narrowing or discontinuation. Martin-Loeches and Torres propose a graded, revisable framework for deciding whether detected microbes cause ICU-acquired pneumonia and for guiding antibiotic reassessment.

title: From fragmentation to fault zone architecture as a structural framework for fault weakening
authors: Nathalie Casas; Guilhem Mollon; Marco Maria Scuderi
abstract: Earthquake nucleation is governed by the evolution of fault zone structure, yet the physical mechanisms linking grain-scale processes to macroscopic weakening remain elusive. Here we use discrete element simulations of quartz-rich gouge in which angular grains fragment dynamically, revealing a robust strain–damage law in which damage accumulates as grains are consumed. Grain size dictates the geometry and timing of localization, while fragmentation enhances compaction and promotes the emergence of a dominant Principal Slip Zone (PSZ). As comminution approaches a saturation state (i.e. minimum grain size), localization can migrate to competing bands, providing a mechanical explanation for overprinted shear fabrics in experiments and natural faults. By linking fragmentation, porosity evolution, and the resulting shear localization, our results provide a local fragmentation state variable for constitutive laws that couple grain-size evolution to fault weakening and the conditions for earthquake nucleation. This study combines simulations and laboratory data to show how grains breaking inside fault gouge reshape fault-zone architecture, focus slip into narrow bands and help faults weaken during deformation.

title: Entropy-driven graded molecular selectivity in stacking-fault-programmed crystalline metallacycle membranes
authors: Runhao Li; Jinlong He; Chen Zhao; Lei Yang; J. L. Wu; Mingzhan Wang; Yi Liu; Yue Ming Sun
abstract: Membrane-based molecular separations are fundamentally constrained by the lack of precisely defined transport pathways, limiting high-flux fractionation of species with subtle size differences. Here, we report a class of stacking-fault-programmed crystalline coordination metallacycle (CCM) membranes featuring programmable nanoarchitectures constructed via interfacial coordination self-assembly. By rationally tuning the angular geometry of metallacyclic precursors, we fabricate two structurally distinct membranes (CCM-1 and CCM-2) possessing ordered microporous frameworks with well-defined transport channels. Both membranes exhibit simultaneously high solvent permeance and sharp molecular sieving, surpassing the conventional permeability-selectivity trade-off. Molecular simulations coupled with thermodynamic analysis reveal that the high selectivity arises from an entropy-dominated transport mechanism, governed by stacking-fault-induced misalignment of metallacycles. This misaligned stacking generates graded steric confinement, enabling precise discrimination between molecules with minimal size differences. Furthermore, we construct a cascade separation system integrating CCM-1 and CCM-2, achieving stepwise fractionation of complex ternary mixtures, including high-value pharmaceutical compounds. The CCM membrane process demonstrates significantly lower costs, carbon emissions, and energy consumption (89% reduction) compared to traditional chromatography and distillation methods. This work establishes stacking-fault programming as a powerful design principle for crystalline membranes, providing a general strategy to engineer entropy-governed transport pathways for energy-efficient and precision separations in chemical and pharmaceutical processes. Membrane based separations can be constrained by the transport pathways in a system. Here the authors design a programmed crystalline coordination metallacycle which self-assembles to form well-defined transport channels.

title: Cell-free reconstitution reveals synergistic stabilization of microtubule doublets by PACRG and FAP20
authors: Daria Khuntsariya; Umut Batman; Arya Krishnan; Souradip Mukherjee; Daniel Rozbeský; Florent Lemaître; Carsten Janke; Virginie Hamel; Paul Guichard; Marcus Braun; Zdeněk Lánský
abstract: Abstract Ciliary microtubule doublets, consisting of an incomplete B-tubule on the surface of a complete A-microtubule, form the fundamental structural framework of motile and sensory cilia/flagella. Ciliary proteins PACRG and FAP20, which are essential for flagellar stability and function, localize to the junction between the A- and the B-tubule. However, their precise role in microtubule doublet assembly and dynamics remains unknown. Here, using a cell-free assay, TIRF-microscopy, and cryo-electron tomography, we demonstrate that in combination PACRG and FAP20 stabilize B-tubule dynamics and microtubule doublet architecture. We show that together these proteins localize to the B-tubules in distinct, high-density patches, which locally stabilize B-tubule by decreasing its depolymerization velocity and increasing its rescue frequency. Cryo-tomography of in vitro reconstructed microtubule doublets in presence of PACRG and FAP20 reveals reduced B-tubule curvature fluctuations, promoting a more rigid and aligned conformation. Altogether, our findings suggest that PACRG and FAP20 function synergistically to reinforce microtubule doublet stability, ensuring ciliary integrity and function.

title: Abrupt permafrost thaw overwhelms vegetation-driven erosion reduction in sediment export on the Tibetan Plateau
authors: Jiapei Ma; Genxu Wang; Chunlin Song; Jinlong Li; Linmao Guo; Kai Li; Peng Huang; Haoyu Wang; Wendong Kang; Zhao Deng; Shouqin Sun
abstract: Vegetation greening and abrupt permafrost thaw are reshaping sediment dynamics across the Tibetan Plateau, yet their relative effects on sediment delivery remain poorly quantified. Here we show that retrogressive thaw slumps are disproportionately important sediment sources, with erosion rates two to three orders of magnitude above undisturbed landscapes and source-to-channel connectivity generally exceeding 60%. Combining multi-decadal satellite observations, high-resolution topographic differencing and cold-region hydrological modelling, we quantify the competing effects of thaw-slump sediment supply and greening-induced erosion reduction. During 2000–2022, thaw slumps delivered more than four times as much non-ice sediment to channels as was reduced by greening, compensating for declining glacier-derived sediment and contributing to increased downstream suspended sediment export. Across permafrost regions, approximately 1.2‰ thaw-slump coverage represents an upper-bound threshold above which thaw-slump sediment delivery exceeds greening-induced sediment reduction. These results show that spatially limited abrupt thaw can outweigh widespread vegetation recovery in regulating sediment delivery from warming permafrost landscapes. Abrupt permafrost degradation through retrogressive thaw slumps can increase sediment delivery to Tibetan rivers, outweighing the greening-induced reduction in sediment export, suggests a study combining multi-decadal satellite observations, topographic differencing, and hydrological modelling.

title: 3D confinement physically regulates cell cycle progression in budding yeast
authors: M Sreepadmanabh; Mridul Gautam; Nikita Bagade; Sunil Laxman; Tapomoy Bhattacharjee
abstract: Our understanding of cell division control traditionally comes via using liquid broths or 2D flat-plate cultures - which cannot recapitulate the complex visco-elasto-plastic properties of natural habitats such as tissues, mucus, and soil. Consequently, how such regimes of physical confinement influence proliferative growth remains poorly understood. Here, using engineered, mechanically tunable and transparent growth matrices, we directly visualize yeast budding and division across 3D viscoelastic regimes. We discover that elevated physical confinement drastically prolongs budding intervals without any physiological defects or activating global regulatory programs. Remarkably, extended cell division times are not associated with transcriptional or proteomic signatures of mechanosensation or cell cycle regulation. Rather, 3D confinement physically constrains the volumetric growth of incipient buds - manifesting as delayed cell cycle progression. Hence, our findings establish that physical constrainment regulates eukaryotic cell division. The eukaryotic cell cycle is highly responsive to genetic, metabolic, and biochemical regulation. But how do the mechanics of complex natural environments influence this fundamental process? This study shows that 3D confinement physically slows down cell division by constraining volumetric growth.

title: Thromboxane A2 receptor signalling amplifies osteoclastogenesis in rheumatoid arthritis through ACSL1 associated mitochondrial oxidative metabolism
authors: Liyan Mei; Xin Li; Siyuan Rao; Chunping Bo; Zifeng Chen; Chuangning Li; 占晨光; Xingrui Yan; Mengyang Ma; Peng Zhang; Yu Wen; Xiang Guo; Bozheng Chen; Meiqi Chen; Xiaodong Wu
abstract: Activated platelets contribute to inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis, but how platelet-derived signals promote bone erosion remains poorly understood. Here we show that thromboxane A2, a major mediator released by activated platelets, promotes the formation of bone-resorbing osteoclasts through the thromboxane A2 receptor. Markers of thromboxane A2 biosynthesis are increased in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, while pharmacological inhibition or genetic loss of its receptor suppresses osteoclastogenesis in mouse cells and mice. Integrated molecular analyses reveal that thromboxane A2 receptor signalling supports osteoclastogenesis by increasing fatty acid oxidation and acetyl-coenzyme A supply needed for mitochondrial energy metabolism, involving peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 beta, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma and acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 1. In male mice, receptor inhibition or genetic deletion reduces osteoclast accumulation and bone destruction. These findings identify thromboxane A2 signalling as a driver of inflammatory bone erosion and a potential therapeutic target in rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Remote sensing of aquatic nutrients from proxy estimation to integration with process models
authors: Chenyi Shi; Xihua Wang; Y. Jun Xu; Xingyu Zhu; Shunqing Jia; Zejun Liu; Boyang Mao; Yan Dai; Yanxin Rong; Qinya Lv; Xuming Ji; Chengming Luo
abstract: Leveraging its capability for large-scale, repeated monitoring, remote sensing has increasingly supported nitrogen and phosphorus estimation in surface waters. However, the evolution of this field from proxy-based nutrient retrieval to integration with process-based models remains insufficiently synthesized. Here we review remote sensing approaches for estimating aquatic nutrients, with emphasis on their roles in supporting process-based modeling, and compare their methodologies, applications, and limitations. At the watershed scale, remote sensing supports land use mapping and pollution load estimation, identifying nutrient sources and constraining transport simulations. At the lake scale, it provides continuous observations and water quality products that inform hydrodynamic and water quality models. At the field and interface scales, remote sensing helps identify hotspots of nutrient loss by capturing the heterogeneity of management practices. Despite these advances, nutrient estimation remains constrained by proxy relationships and spatial scale. Future research should integrate remote sensing with hydrodynamic and biogeochemical models to constrain nutrient fluxes and improve mechanistic understanding of aquatic nutrient cycling. At the watershed scale, remote sensing maps land use and estimates pollution loads; at the lake scale, it provides water quality data for models; at field and interface scales, it identifies nutrient-loss hotspots, based on a review of remote sensing to approaches aquatic nutrients.

title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
authors: Guanna Pan; Ulrike Kornek; Chen Chris Gong; Edna Johanna Molina Bacca; Gunnar Luderer; Ottmar Edenhofer
abstract: Abstract Climate change mitigation reshapes the distribution of economic assets in the low-carbon transition. Here we quantify climate-related assets for 169 countries across four dimensions: fossil fuel production, climate change damages, renewable energy potential and land carbon sequestration capacity. We combine integrated assessment models, climate projections, economic damage functions and biosphere datasets to assess asset changes under multiple mitigation scenarios. Geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise from climate change mitigation because losses and gains across energy and environmental assets are country-specific, which we further characterize through a broad clustering and a detailed pairwise similarity analysis. Our analysis suggests comparatively moderate impacts for the USA, the European Union and China, highlighting the challenge that the largest economic powers may not be those with the strongest asset-based interest for climate action. While our framework remains limited, our data provide input for integrating other ethical, governance and socioeconomic factors in future analyses of opportunities and challenges for ambitious climate change mitigation.

title: Nickel isotopes in Apollo and Chang’e soils reveal widespread micrometeorite-driven processing of the lunar regolith
authors: Ke Zhu; Maosheng Yang; Jun Huang; Wei Tian; Meng‐Hua Zhu; Tim Elliott
abstract: Abstract Micrometeorite bombardment is a fundamental surface process on the Moon and other airless bodies, driving elemental evaporation, isotopic fractionation, and material mixing in surface regoliths. Here, we report high-precision stable Ni isotope data for lunar soils returned by the Apollo (11, 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17) and Chang’e (5 and 6) missions, covering geographically and geologically diverse lunar terrains. The analyzed soils show δ 60/58 Ni values of 0.345‰ to 1.280‰ (relative to NIST SRM 986), generally heavier than lunar basalts and the inferred bulk silicate Moon, indicating widespread heavy Ni isotope enrichment during surface processing. Together with published Chang’e-5 drill-core data, these results demonstrate that micrometeorite-driven Ni isotope fractionation is widespread across the lunar surface. Local variability, however, reflects additional controls. The relatively low δ 60/58 Ni values of the immature Apollo 12 soils are consistent with limited cumulative micrometeorite processing, whereas the mature Apollo 16 soils have high Ni concentrations and Ni/Co ratios, indicating additional compositional overprinting by Ni-rich material. Stable Ni isotopes, particularly when combined with regolith maturity and Ni/Co ratios, therefore provide a sensitive tracer of micrometeorite-driven lunar surface processing and its local overprinting.

title: Myosin filaments of vertebrate skeletal and cardiac muscle are highly similar, but not identical
authors: Pouria Gholami Tilko; Hosna Rastegarpouyani; Behrouz Ghazi Esfahani; Jose Renato Pinto; Kenneth A. Taylor
abstract: Striated muscles consist of two filament types, one based on actin, one based on myosin. All striated muscle actin filaments are highly similar. Invertebrate myosin filaments are heterogeneous; those of vertebrates are homogeneous. Mouse and human cardiac muscle myosin filaments are highly similar. How similar are they to those of skeletal muscle? Using Mavacamten for myosin head stabilization, we find the relaxed thick filaments of rabbit skeletal, human cardiac and mouse cardiac muscles are highly similar, differing primarily in the positioning of myosin binding protein C domains, C5-C7. In isolated cardiac thick filaments, C5-C7 lie along the filament backbone. In mouse and human cardiac myofibrils, C7 extends radially toward the thin filament. Here we show in isolated rabbit skeletal muscle thick filaments, C7 also extends outward but with C6 bending azimuthally to position C5 onto titin suggesting a thick filament architecture highly adaptable to multiple functions with relatively simple structural changes. The least understood muscle filament contains myosin. How similar are myosin filaments across muscle types and species? Here the authors show rabbit skeletal and human cardiac thick filaments are highly similar, demonstrating an architecture highly adaptable with simple structural changes

title: Global proteolysis during starvation governs proteome remodeling and a survival–regrowth trade-off in bacteria
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: Gabriel Manzanarez; Rohan Balakrishnan; Harish Kannan; Miriam Abele; Hiroyuki Okano; Fukang She; Zhongge Zhang; Chenhao Wu; Lance Freiman; Christina Ludwig; Matteo Mori; Terence Hwa B
abstract: , carbon starvation triggers large-scale proteome remodeling, with global proteolysis supplying both the amino acids (AAs) and ATP for protein synthesis. This remodeling occurs in two phases, with a short preparatory phase relying on constitutive proteolytic machinery and fueled by residual carbon waste, and a more extended phase, relying on starvation-induced protein components synthesized during the preparatory phase and fueled by AA catabolism. The starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) program dominating the extended phase depends on YeaG, a little-known, broadly conserved protein highly expressed in stationary phase under the control of the general stress sigma factor RpoS. SPD fuels the synthesis of stress proteins, including those in the RpoS regulon and AA catabolic enzymes, markedly enhancing survival and accounting for much of the viability benefit conferred by RpoS during carbon starvation. However, in mutants where an energy source can be supplemented without enabling biomass growth, SPD and the accompanying protein synthesis are largely dispensable for survival, indicating that a primary physiological function of the synthesized stress proteins is to conserve or recycle energy during carbon starvation. Because SPD targets biosynthetic enzymes nonspecifically, proteome remodeling via SPD imposes a fundamental trade-off between long-term survival and short-term metabolic activity, manifested as a lag before regrowth upon nutrient replenishment. Together, these findings establish SPD as a general physiological strategy shaping protein synthesis and survival in nongrowing bacteria.

title: Evidence of vertical soil hydraulic heterogeneity regulating hydrothermal simulations in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands
authors: Rong Liu; Xin Wang; Zuoliang Wang; Yongjie Pan; Yan Song
abstract: Abstract. Alpine wetlands on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau host vertically structured and highly contrasting pore systems that fundamentally shape land and atmosphere exchanges, yet their hydraulic expressions and process implications remain poorly quantified. This study provides the first process based and depth resolved characterization of these layered pore structures using soil physical analyses and laboratory evaporation experiments. The derived Clapp–Hornberger parameters reveal coherent hydraulic contrasts, with surface layers dominated by macropore connectivity and showing high θs and Ks and low b that promote rapid drainage and evaporation, mid layer domains with lower θs and Ks and larger b that enhance retention in finer pores, and deeper layers that act as stable and persistent storage reservoirs. These properties together generate a vertical regime of rapid near surface drainage, delayed mid layer release, and long lasting deep moisture storage. When implemented in Noah-MP, this hydraulic stratification systematically altered water and energy partitioning during wet and dry periods and showed that vertical hydraulic heterogeneity rather than a single layer parameterization governs the timing and magnitude of evaporation and heat fluxes. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence that pore scale structure regulates profile scale hydrothermal responses in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau wetlands and establish a physically grounded basis for representing vertically heterogeneous hydraulic processes in land surface models.

title: Electronic tuning of dynamic imine bonds enables programmable pore gating in metal–organic frameworks
authors: Meng Qiao; Youcong Li; Shengcun Chen; Sirui Liu; Yu‐Hao Gu; Dong Zhang; Yifan Liu; Lei Gao; Mengting Chang; Xing Zhang; Shuai Yuan
abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising host matrices for molecular encapsulation, yet their application is often limited by fixed pore apertures that exclude guest molecules larger than the pore openings. Herein, we overcome this limitation by electronic tuning of dynamic imine bonds to induce reversible pore gating that transiently expands framework accessibility beyond its intrinsic aperture. By incorporating imine-based linkers bearing electron-donating/withdrawing substituents into a robust Zr-based MOF scaffold via postsynthetic linker exchange, we systematically modulate imine dissociation equilibria while preserving crystallinity. A linear correlation between Hammett substituent constants and imine bond stability establishes electronic effects as a predictive handle for programming framework dynamics. Systematic variation of substituents establishes an optimal metastable regime in which reversible linker dissociation permits size-adaptive guest uptake without structural degradation. As a proof of concept, paclitaxel and other therapeutics are efficiently encapsulated, and the resulting materials exhibit good biocompatibility together with programmable, environment-responsive release kinetics under physiological conditions. Guided by electronic effects, this study programs the dynamics of reversible imine bonds in metal-organic frameworks, enabling adaptive pore opening for efficient drug loading and controlled release.

title: Drivers of the likelihood of evolutionary rescue in response to novel infectious diseases
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
authors: Laurinne J. Balstad; Marissa L. Baskett
abstract: The introduction of novel infectious diseases has caused significant declines in many species, and in some cases, local extinction. Simultaneously, hosts might adapt to these novel pathogens, allowing population recovery, an example of evolutionary rescue (ER). Novel infectious diseases differ from sudden, abiotic stressors in that disease only impacts a subset of individuals within the population and individuals might be affected for a finite period. Whether ER occurs in an infectious disease context, and how likely it is relative to abiotic stress, might depend on both host and pathogen characteristics such as the scale of transmission (e.g., local density-dependent transmission only or additional infection through an external reservoir), the degree of fatality or immunity, and the adaptive pathway in terms of whether adaptive alleles reduce mortality, reduce likelihood of infection, or enhance recovery. Here, we use a stochastic mathematical model of host-pathogen dynamics with evolution of a novel allele conferring disease robustness to quantify how population trajectories, including the probability of and time to ER, vary across adaptive pathways and disease characteristics. We find that ER is more likely to occur with dynamical disease transmission compared to a lasting stressor that affects the entire population, indicating that protecting a subset of the population from stress facilitates ER. Among cases with disease transmission, ER is generally more likely to occur with the adaptation of mortality-blocking alleles and sources of transmission that include an external reservoir.

title: Designing nonlinear perturbative metamaterials that compute
authors: Sima Zahedi Fard; Paolo Tiso; Parisa Omidvar; Marc Serra‐Garcia
abstract: Designing metamaterials that compute is challenging; the space of possible geometries is very large, and the relation between structure and function is complex. Perturbative metamaterials, consisting of weakly interacting unit cells, can be efficiently designed by combining simple geometric building blocks. However, perturbative metamaterials are conventionally defined in terms of linear wave physics, which prevents their use in information-processing applications that require nonlinearity. Here, we introduce a nonlinear formulation for perturbative metamaterials that allows us to identify material geometries that perform target computations. The design is enabled by a nonlinear, localized map connecting metamaterial deformations to a discrete tight-binding model that encodes the computation. We demonstrate the generality of this approach by designing three information-processing metamaterials based on three different computing paradigms: an Ising machine that solves combinatorial optimization problems through energy minimization, a mechanical racetrack device for in-memory computing, and a speech classification metamaterial based on analog neuromorphic computing. Elastic metamaterials provide opportunities for implementing computation tasks, yet generality provides a major challenge with respect to the design of metamaterial geometry. Here, the authors introduce a two-step metamaterial design strategy embedding first the computation functionality in a tight-binding model and subsequently tailoring a metamaterial geometry.

title: Dendritic computation bridges neuroscience and foundation models
authors: Man Yao; Yuqi Pan; Yiran Zhong; Shijie Mei; Zhen Qin; Kexin Wang; Jiakui Hu; Siyu Ding; Tianxiang Hu; Yanbin Huang; Guoqi Li; Lei Deng; Zhong Zheng; Mingqiang Huang; Xuyang Shen
abstract: A prevailing view holds that although neuroscience historically inspired AI, its role in the recent evolution of AI, driven by the scaling of foundation models, is minor. We challenge this perspective by establishing a biological analogy between simplified dendritic neuron models and the attention mechanisms central to AI foundation models. We show that AI attention mechanisms bear direct mappings to internal neuronal complexities arising from dendritic organization, rather than to the mere inter-neuronal connections of simple point neurons. This re-conceptualization not only offers a neuroscience-informed perspective for understanding core AI methodologies beyond their formulation as abstract mathematical operations, but also paves the way for neuro-inspired foundation models that leverage neuroscientific insights to sustainably advance modern AI beyond scaling laws. As an example of this paradigm, we introduce a dendritic-inspired complexity framework, and design a hybrid-attention foundation model with dendritic-inspired sparse computation, which enhances memory capacity while reducing computational demands. Our model supports a 50M context window-equivalent to roughly 40 volumes of Shakespeare-demonstrating superior long-term memory capabilities. This work pioneers a paradigm that harnesses intra-neuronal dynamics to drive sustained advances in modern AI, while also offering a potential route to understanding dendritic computational mechanisms. How insights from neuroscience can inform future AI foundation models is an active area of exploration. Here, the authors show that AI attention mechanisms resemble dendritic computations within individual neurons rather than interactions between neurons, inspiring a dendritic-inspired model with improved long-term memory and reduced computational cost.

title: Closed-loop upcycling of residual lithium in LiFePO4 into tunable thin lithium metal electrodes
authors: Keyu Zheng; Jiashu Yuan; Said Amzil; Shuangshuang Wang; Yinghui Li; Shunjie Xu; Wenhao Jia; Le Huang; Lei Zhang; Jin Zhu; Linjun Luo; Jie Gao; Yongyao Xia; Yonggao Xia
abstract: Abstract With the rapid development of electric vehicles, massive quantities of spent lithium iron phosphate batteries are generated, creating an urgent demand for efficient and sustainable recycling. Here we show a redox mediator-assisted strategy that directly converts simulated spent lithium iron phosphate powder into thin lithium metal, reducing energy requirements and enabling regeneration of the redox mediator. The process achieves a 98% final lithium extraction and produces lithium foils with a preformed interphase, tolerating volume changes and resisting air corrosion. The recycled Li (4.14 mAh cm −2 ) enables Li | |Li cells to cycle over 1,200 h at the test condition of 1 mA cm −2 / 1 mAh cm −2 and shows stable interfacial resistance with reduced electrolyte decomposition. When paired with NCM811, the cells retain 91.4% capacity over 400 cycles at 0.2 C/0.3 C. This closed-loop process couples lithium recovery with designed electrode fabrication, providing an alternative pathway for sustainable battery recycling and negative electrode design.

title: A multi-model analysis of hydrogen uptake in a climate-neutral Europe
authors: Amirhossein Fattahi; Mobi van der Linden; Francesco Dalla Longa; Bob van der Zwaan; Mark Dekker; Harmen Sytze de Boer; Francesco Davide Sanvito; Stefan Pfenninger; Robert Pietzcker; Renato Rodrigues; Behnam Zakeri; Muhammad Awais; Daniel Huppmann; Sonja Sechi; Panagiotis F. Fragkos
abstract: Using an ensemble of integrated assessment models, we quantify the role of hydrogen in Europe’s energy transition under multiple climate policy scenarios. Hydrogen uptake in our net-zero scenario varies widely across models, ranging from 0.3 to 11.7 exajoules (average 4 exajoules) by 2050 and corresponding to 1-14% (average 7%) of final energy consumption, primarily in industry and synthetic fuel production. Hydrogen contributes minimally to electricity generation, and its direct use in transport and buildings remains limited. Despite projected carbon dioxide prices of 150–250 euros per tonne by 2030, hydrogen adoption remains below 2% (7 million tonnes) of final energy consumption, far below the European Union’s 2030 target of 20 million tonnes of green hydrogen from domestic production and imports. Hydrogen trade is scarcely modelled and therefore underrepresented. Our results support prioritizing near-term electrification while preparing strategically today for large-scale hydrogen expansion after 2040. Across multiple European energy models, deep decarbonization relies on strong early electrification, while hydrogen expands mainly after 2040 in hard-to-abate sectors; stronger policy support is essential for robust net-zero pathways.

title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
authors: Angus M. O’Ferrall; David Lally; Peter Makaula; Gladys Namacha; Joseph M. Lewis; Patrick Musicha; Richard N. Goodman; Ellie Allman; Sabrina John Moyo; Claire S. Waddington; Sekeleghe Amos Kayuni; Nicholas Feasey; Janelisa Musaya; J. Russell Stothard; Adam Paul Roberts
abstract: Abstract Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8–41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0–62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

title: Universal crystallization kinetics of solution-processed semiconductors
authors: Zhitian Ling; Mateusz Brzeziński; Shuanglong Wang; Konstantinos Bidinakis; Lei Gao; Chongyao Li; Xin Zhou; Hai I. Wang; Stefan A. L. Weber; Paul W. M. Blom; Wojciech Pisula; Tomasz Marszałek
abstract: Heterogeneous crystallization kinetics critically govern the morphology and performance of solution-processed semiconductors, yet morphology control is often achieved through trial-and-error optimization. Quantitative understanding of crystallization is essential for precise morphology control but is limited by the simultaneous occurrence of heterogeneous nucleation and crystal growth. Here, a time-defined induced nucleation strategy has been developed to initiate crystallization at specific stages of solution processing. Systematic variation of nucleation timing reveals three distinct morphological regimes, whose emergence is explained by the concentration-dependent critical cluster radius in bulk, interfacial, and cusp environments. On this basis, a quantitative, dimensionless model is developed for heterogeneous crystallization kinetics across diverse processing conditions. The model demonstrates universality across perovskite and organic semiconductors. In situ studies reveal identical growth kinetics for induced and spontaneous nuclei, validating its generality. The resulting morphology control enables tuning of crystallinity and charge transport in solution-processed transistors.

title: Surface carbonation governs olivine reactivity for rapid CO2 mineralization
authors: Zihua Shao; Yunfeng Liang; Gyuhwan Jo; K. Nakamura; Takeshi Tsuji
abstract: Abstract Ultramafic rocks are a global resource with vast potential for permanent CO 2 mineralization. However, the origin of the striking reactivity difference between Ca- and Mg-bearing olivine remains poorly understood. Here we show that this difference arises not merely from the type of cation, but more fundamentally from how these cations modulate the oxygen reactivity. Nonbridging oxygens serve as the oxygen source for CO 2 surface reactions, which in Ca-olivine reduce the Ca 2+ dissolution barrier by 60% and accelerate ion release by six orders of magnitude. The calculated apparent dissolution rate constants reproduce the experimentally observed complete conversion of Ca-olivine within hours under 1 atm CO 2 . This multiscale framework reveals how surface reactions govern silicate carbonation and provides a predictive basis for modeling and engineering large-scale CO 2 mineralization in both synthetic materials and basaltic reservoirs.

title: Spontaneous ferromagnetic Fe–La geminal atoms with spin and coordination modulation for acidic oxygen reduction
authors: Fanpeng Kong; Qing Gong; Bingbao Mei; Cong Kang; Jinyu Ye; Chunyu Du; 尹鸽平; Juncai Dong; Shenlong Zhao
abstract: Synergistic spin-state and local coordination engineering offers a promising strategy for enhancing the acidic oxygen reduction reaction performance of Fe–N–C electrocatalysts, yet the precise control and stabilization of active sites remain challenging. Here we report a Fe–La geminal-atom electrocatalyst (Fe1-La1/NC) with spontaneous ferromagnetic spin ordering for acidic oxygen reduction reaction. The catalyst achieves a half-wave potential of 0.92 V and a turnover frequency of 17.3e-site−1s−1, compared with commercial Pt/C (0.87 V, 9.9e-site−1s−1). A proton exchange membrane fuel cell equipped with Fe1-La1/NC cathode delivers a high current density of 56 mA cm−2 at 0.9ViR-free under H2-O2 condition, while maintaining stable operation for 100 h at 0.67 V with 86% performance retention. Operando studies and theoretical simulations reveal that La incorporation promotes a spin-polarized high-spin Fe 3 d configuration and room-temperature ferromagnetic ordering, while also regulating the local coordination/electronic structure and oxygen-intermediate adsorption. Moreover, La enables dynamic self-adaptive stabilization of Fe sites, which mitigates the conventional activity–stability trade-off. This finding provides an avenue to rationally design efficient and selective electrocatalysts. Developing robust Fe–N–C catalysts that unite activity and durability remains challenging for acidic oxygen reduction. Here, the authors report spontaneous ferromagnetic Fe–La geminal atoms that create high-spin Fe sites and a spin pinning effect for fuel-cell catalysis.

title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
authors: Abelardo Aguilar; Ingrid Miranda Perez; Omer Nadel; Stephen Nayfach; Luis Ruiz Pestana; Anca Mara Segall; Forest L. Rohwer; Simon Roux; Simon J. White; Antoni Luque
abstract: The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

title: Replacing anaerobic fermentation with reverse β-oxidation enables growth-coupled evolution for enhanced fatty-alcohol production
authors: Bridgie Cawthon; Aidan E. Cowan; Zen Yoshikawa; Kenneth Low; Justin J. Baerwald; Nawa Raj Baral; Matthew R. Incha; Jennifer  W. Gin; Yan Chen; Christopher J. Petzold; Edward E. K. Baidoo; Emine A. Turumtay; Corinne D. Scown; Adam M. Feist; Jay D. Keasling
abstract: Abstract Engineering robust fermentation hosts remains a barrier to scalable biomanufacturing. In this work we replace canonical mixed-acid fermentation in Escherichia coli with a redox‑balanced reverse β‑oxidation (rBOX) pathway that produces medium‑chain fatty alcohols and is bioenergetically equivalent to ethanol fermentation. This synthetic fermentation restores anaerobic growth, tightly coupling fitness to product formation and enabling adaptive laboratory evolution that selects for mutations increasing rBOX flux. Evolved strains increase maximum productivity fourfold (110 ± 0.15 mg/L/hr) and titer more than threefold up to 4.0 ± 0.28 g/L compared to the unevolved strain. Proteomic analyses of evolved strains indicate differential expression of enzymes at key metabolic nodes and activation of latent genes with functions overlapping those of rBOX enzymes. These results establish redox-balanced growth coupling as a powerful tool for strain improvement and demonstrate rBOX as a practical synthetic fermentation pathway.

title: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
authors: Hugo Moreira; Emilie Bruand; Craig D. Storey; James R. Darling; Mike Fowler; Marine Cotte; Fleurice Parat; Lorraine Tual; Bruno Dhuime
abstract: Abstract In the modern Earth, sub-arc mantle oxygen fugacity is intrinsically associated with addition of sulfur species by slab fluids. However, it is unclear to what extent recycling of volatiles controlled redox changes of the sub-arc mantle in the early Earth. Here we use sulfur K-edge micro-X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy to measure the relative abundances of S 6+ , S 4+ and S 2− in apatite inclusions hosted by geochemically characterized and dated zircons from sub-arc sanukitoid magmas that span 3.4 billion years of Earth’s geological history. The sub-arc mantle shows marked increase in oxygen fugacity between 3.4 and 3.0 billion years ago (Ga). It is substantially more oxidized than unaltered ambient upper mantle, a characteristic that cannot be explained by fractionation, degassing or intrinsic mantle processes. We propose that progressive oxidative weathering enhanced the proportion of oxidized sulfur recycled to mantle wedge sources, establishing feedback between subduction of surface materials and incrementally oxidized arc magmatism. Early subduction involving inorganic oxidation and ‘whiffs’ of oxygen between 3.4 and 2.7 Ga may have regulated an early increase in fugacity of the sub-arc mantle before the Great Oxidation Event, matching similar conditions to the modern Earth by 2.1 Ga.

title: Plasmonic metasurface microfluidic accelerates redox reactions for rapid phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing
authors: Roozbeh Siavash Moakhar; Mahsa Jalali; Tamer AbdElFatah; Sripadh Guptha Yedire; Max Petkun; Carolina del Real Mata; Ziwei He; Hamed Shieh; Geoffrey A. McKay; Rachel Corsini; Grace Reszetnik; Seyed Vahid Hamidi; Sahar Sadat Mahshid; Cédric P. Yansouni; Dao M. Nguyen
abstract: Electron-accepting chain reactions play crucial roles in diagnostics for bacterial infections, from nucleic acid amplification for bacterial identification to metabolic assays for phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing. When coupled with redox mediators, these reactions can be interrogated using an electroanalytical method. We demonstrate kinetic acceleration of loop-mediated isothermal amplification-based identification and resazurin-based phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility profiling through enhanced electromagnetic fields and modulated hot electron injection at the multilayered plasmonic metasurface-fluidic interface. We systematically investigate rounded versus sharp-apex plasmonic architectures, quantifying near-field magnitude and decay to identify geometries that maximize kinetic amplification under electrochemical readout. This approach is further combined with machine learning-assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. In a prospective pilot clinical study of urine specimens directly from patients with suspected urinary tract infections, we observe high accuracy and strong essential and categorical agreement with standard clinical microbiology assays for bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

title: Origami-inspired folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels for thermal insulation
authors: Xuanyu Chen; Zhao Yuan; Zhijun Zhang; Chi Hu; Shuangfei Wang; Chongxing Huang
abstract: Nanofiber aerogels (NFAs) are promising thermal insulation materials for extreme environments; however, simultaneously achieving mechanical robustness, resilience, and low thermal conductivity remains a long-standing challenge in layered NFAs, where interlaminar instability often compromises structural reliability. Here we present an origami-inspired structural engineering strategy to construct folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels. A folded-interlocked origami skeleton, integrated with a tailored interlaminar structure, introduces geometric confinement and fiber-mediated interlaminar toughening. As a result, the aerogels exhibit high compressive strength (548.02 kPa at 80% strain) and a near-zero Poisson’s ratio. Importantly, the robust interlaminar network enhances resistance to delamination, allowing the aerogels to sustain tensile deformation up to approximately 40% strain before interlaminar failure. Meanwhile, interlaminar-guided heat-flow redistribution yields a low axial thermal conductivity of 0.035 W m−1 K−1 and pronounced anisotropic thermal insulation. This work provides an architectural strategy for designing folded-interlocked NFAs for thermal protection in aerospace and other harsh environments. Chen et al. report origami-inspired folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels that combine mechanical resilience with low axial thermal conductivity through geometric confinement and an interlaminar fibrous network.

title: Orientation tomography of lanthanide-doped nanoprobes by polarization-resolved micro-spectroscopy
authors: Lilian Magermans; Marcello Bonetti; Thierry Gacoin; Jongwook Kim
abstract: Abstract Quantifying three-dimensional (3D) orientation is critical for understanding self-assembly and collective behavior in soft matter and biological systems. Moreover, orientational analysis of anisotropic particles can characterize locally applied forces in fluids. We present a methodology for 3D orientation tomography based on polarization-resolved spectroscopy of lanthanide-doped nanorods exhibiting multiple emission dipoles, enabling 3D orientation measurements from a single viewing angle. We develop a confocal imaging setup optimized for lanthanide luminescence and a theoretical framework to extract both the local director and order parameter in nanorod assemblies. The technique achieves 0.5 μm lateral and 1 μm axial spatial resolution and is demonstrated in dense nematic liquid-crystal assemblies, resolving complex 3D topological structures, and in microfluidic flows, mapping alignment under hydrodynamic shear. This approach provides a versatile platform for quantitative studies of collective orientation, self-assembly mechanics, and alignment induced by external forces, and can be extended to other lanthanide-labeled particles and molecular probes.

title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
authors: Thomas Ulrich; Xiaoyu Zou; Mathilde Marchandon; Nico Schliwa; Fengzhou Tan; Alice‐Agnes Gabriel; Wenyuan Fan; Peter M. Shearer; Myo Thant; Tha Zin Htet Tin; Eric O. Lindsey; Yuri A. Fialko
abstract: Abstract The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

title: Nanoconfinement-cooperated catalysis enables rapid tandem redox kinetics for wide-temperature lithium-sulfur batteries
authors: Tianli Li; Tao Chen; Pu Hu; Congcong Cai; Juntao Wang; Chaoqun Shang; Liwei Xiong; Yajie Li; Hanxing Liu; Jian Wang; Yaobing Wang
abstract: The slow kinetics of sulfur cathodes caused by the high energy barriers of Li + desolvation stem primarily from the structure of the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). Herein, a synergistic strategy combining electrochemical tandem catalysis with spatial nanoconfinement is proposed to regulate the Li(solvent) x + dynamics. As a proof-of-concept, the porous covalent organic framework (denoted as TPBD) decorated MXene is in situ constructed, acting as a tandem kinetic promoter. The theoretical simulations and in situ Raman reveal that the porous TPBD layer confines the bulky Li(solvent) x + species and sieves the spatial structure with accelerated Li + diffusion kinetics. Meanwhile, MXene serves as a negatively charged substrate that helps disrupt anion-solvent interactions and reconstruct the solvation structure at the IHP, thereby enhancing Li + kinetics and sulfur redox reversibility. Encouragingly, the assembled cells demonstrate a superior Li + transference number (0.77), long-term cycling lifespan up to 1000 cycles, as well as excellent areal capacity (>6 mAh cm −2 ) at 0°C and superior rate capability at 50°C under a high sulfur loading of 7.51 mg cm −2 . The as-prepared pouch cell remains stable for over 100 cycles, validating this novel integration of catalysis and nanoconfinement for tandem kinetics in Li-S batteries.

title: Learning to infer transitively on a mental line in premotor cortex
authors: Sofia Raglio; Gabriele Di Antonio; Emiliano Brunamonti; Stefano Ferraina; Maurizio Mattia
abstract: Transitive inference (TI) is a form of deductive reasoning that enables the derivation of unknown relationships among premises. It is hypothesized that this cognitive process relies on mapping stimuli onto a "mental line," a linear workspace organized by arbitrarily assigned ranks. However, its neural basis remains unclear: Does this mental line have a neural correlate and how is it learned? This study investigates the role of dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) in encoding the hypothesized mental line as monkeys acquire item relationships for motor decisions. Findings reveal that PMd multiunit activity organizes along a theoretically predicted direction, supporting a geometrical model that explains behavior. Moreover, a learning process is observed, where the mental line rotates to align with motor planning.

title: Geochemical clustering reveals cryptic eruptions and tephra correlations from Antarctic fumarolic ice-cave archives
authors: Paola Del Carlo; Paola Del Carlo; Alessandro Musu; Alessio Di Roberto; Giuseppe Re; Gaetano Giudice; Mónica Ágreda López; Maurizio Petrelli
abstract: Abstract Volcanic deposits preserved within Antarctic fumarolic ice caves provide rare access to sub-ice eruptive records hidden beneath the ice cap. Here we present the first integrated textural, petrological, and geochemical characterisation of 21 tephra samples from three summit ice caves at Mount Melbourne (Northern Victoria Land, Antarctica). Major and trace-element glass compositions, combined with published datasets, were analysed using multivariate statistical workflows. Dimensionality reduction and clustering identified a distinct compositional group with no known equivalent in the existing Mount Melbourne record, suggesting that at least one previously unrecognised Holocene eruption occurred within the investigated Fumarolic Ice Caves. Correspondence between Fumarolic Ice Cave deposits and volcanic signatures in marine sediment, englacial sequences, and other proximal-distal records refined Mount Melbourne’s eruptive history and strengthened tephra correlations across archives. More broadly, sub-ice tephra archives can reveal hidden eruptive histories relevant to volcanic hazard assessment in polar regions.

title: From scrap to prime: Designing high-performance alloys from dirty feedstocks with machine learning
authors: Chao Yang; Bo Peng; Binhan Sun; Qingzhou Tao; Yuxin Zeng; Lijun Zhang; Da Shu; Jian Lü; Dierk Raabe; Liuliu Han; Wei Ye
abstract: Producing alloys from recycled metals via secondary synthesis can markedly cut energy use, greenhouse-gas emissions, and dependence on scarce, strategically important elements relative to primary routes. The central obstacle is the feedstock itself: Scrap is chemically heterogeneous and unpredictable, a "dirty" mix whose impurities typically embrittle materials. Conventional strategies address this challenge by diluting impurities through the addition of virgin material, thereby restricting scrap utilization, limiting microstructural design freedom, and undermining cost and sustainability benefits. Here, we introduce a fundamentally different, data-driven paradigm that deliberately reverses a five-millennia-old metallurgical injunction: Rather than purifying the alloy, we design the alloy to accommodate and exploit its contaminants. Using a model ductile iron representative of 120 million metric tons of heavily contaminated scrap, we couple experiments with deep-neural-network optimization to identify chemically robust, impurity-tolerant processing windows. The resulting "dirty" irons retain ductility and strength by integrating impurity effects into a purposeful microstructure, rather removing them. The approach achieves complete recyclability, an 8.1% reduction in manufacturing cost, and mechanical gains of up to 15.2% in ultimate tensile strength and 73.2% in elongation at fracture. Crucially, it overcomes the canonical strength-ductility trade-off while enabling far greater scrap utilization and material circularity. By endowing alloys with a practical "gene of scrap compatibility," this strategy reframes alloy design for a resource-constrained future and advances a mass-conserving circular economy for metals.

title: From ancient practice to modern innovation solving the clay mineral puzzle in brickmaking
authors: Sen Wang; Lloyd Gainey; Lihui Liu; Zijun Zeng; Shusheng Xiao; Runliang Zhu; Sara Jane Couperthwaite; Yuantong Gu; Yunfei Xi
abstract: Abstract Clay minerals are the most crucial constituents in brickmaking clays, yet the specific role of different clay minerals remain poorly understood due to their natural coexistence and formidable challenges of separation. Here, we design a kaolinite-illite-quartz-feldspar system through a multiple-stage purification strategy, enabling direct evaluation of two of the most critical clay minerals for brick making - kaolinite and illite. Precise tuning the initial clay mineral assemblage yields brick strengths up to 8.5 times the ASTM C62 Grade MW requirement, without upgrading existing production methods. Mineralogical mechanisms responsible for substantial strength enhancement are revealed. Extensive analyses of 60 brick formulations uncovered a breakdown of conventional linear relationships among different brick properties due to the temperature-dependent responses of kaolinite and illite; specific formation pathways of mullite and amorphous phases; and over-firing defects above 1200 °C due to K + -induced fluxing from illite. Notably, a previously unrecognized negative correlation between mullite and brick strength is identified, suggesting a need to reconsider the widely held assumption of mullite as a strengthening phase. This work not only presents insights for optimizing high-strength brick formulations but also opens avenues for investigating the intricate contributions of distinct starting components to key brick performance.
